reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The manuscript by Meng et al reported the critical role of the UFL1-AKT axis in breast cancer progression and drug
resistance. Specifically, the authors found that AKT1 was UFMylated by UFL1, an UFMylation-specific E3 ligase, in breast
cancer cells. AKT1 UFMylation promoted its ER recruitment and activation by both PDK1 and mTORC2, which in turn
enhanced lipid biogenesis and cancer progression. Moreover, the authors showed that AKT1 phosphorylated UFL1 and
boosted UFL1’s activity. Finally, UFL1 expression was elevated in breast cancer samples and associated with poor
prognosis in human patients. Targeting both UFMylation and AKT1 had a synergetic effect on TNBC in xenograft models.
Overall, the finding of the positive feed-back regulation between AKT1 and UFL1 appears to be novel and may represent a
potential target for cancer therapy. However, there are some significant flaws in data analysis and interpretation that should
be addressed. As described below, this reviewer failed to duplicate some of the results as claimed by the authors regarding
the association between UFL1 mRNA level and overall survival of human BC patients. In addition, a few pieces of
experimental data appeared to conflict to each other, and some results were difficult to explain. Finally, the evidence to
support the role of lipid metabolism in tumor progression is relatively insufficient.
Specific comments:
1. Concerns on bioinformatic analyses of BC databases and clinical samples.
a. This reviewer failed to duplicate KM survival curves using GEPIA database (http://gepia.cancer-pku.cn). A simple search
using UFL1 and BRCA dataset in GEPIA yielded no significant association between Ufl1 mRNA levels and overall survival
of BC patients. The number of patients also differed from what the authors reported.
b. In Fig.S1C, GSE9693 dataset was about “Clostridioides difficile”, which was nothing to do with breast cancer.
c. In Fig.1F, this reviewer could not replicate the KM survival plot as reported using KM plotter database (kmplot.com). There
was no reference or GSE number for Liu-2014 dataset (as indicated in Fig.1F). Additionally, none of BC datasets in KMplot
could generate similar survival plots showing the significant correlation between Ufl1 mRNA level and overall survival.
Please provide more information on the dateset and UFL1 (named as KIAA0776 in KM plot) probe set used in the analysis
reported by the authors.
2. Specificity of Ufl1 antibody in IHC
The authors did not provide the source of UFL1 and other antibodies. To the knowledge of this reviewer, some commercial
UFL1 antibodies recognized multiple bands in immunoblotting. Even though Fig.1K may have indirectly addressed this
issue, more stringent test should be done to examine the specificity of UFL1 antibody. Meanwhile, the knockdown efficiency
of UFL1 shRNAs should be shown.
3. For cell death assay of tissue culture cells, Annexin V staining or TUNEL should be done in addition
to CC3 staining.
4. The claim that UFL1 is an oncogenic driver (Fig.1) appears to be an overstatement. Even though UFL1 overexpression
promoted cell proliferation, no experimental evidence supported its oncogenic activity.
5. The claim that UFL1 promotes breast cancer cell growth by increasing lipid accumulation was backed up by the only
functional assay that was shown in Fig.S2J and K, in which addition of OA reversed UFL1 knockdown phenotype. Since
lipid metabolism was such a big part of this study, more functional experiments should be done to firmly establish the
relationship between lipid metabolism, the UFL1-AKT axis and tumor progression.
6. High-quality of confocal imaging in Fig.3F should be provided. The current one appeared to be fuzzy, especially
UFL1.
7. As shown in Fig.3I and J, knockdown of UFL1 led to reduced AKT UFMylation but had no effect on overall UFMylation
(especially RPL26 UFMylation, around 27kD and higher), a result that seems to contradict to previous studies.
Please explain why.
8. In Fig.3I and J and other similar figures, please provide the results of IgGs as negative controls in those IPs.
9. In Fig.3, it was showed that UFM1 antibody could detect UFMylated endogenous and exogenous AKT1. How about AKT1
and Flag antibodies?
10. In Fig. 4A and B, it would be interesting to examine if phosphorylation of other mTORC2 and PDK1 targets is altered by
UFL1 knockdown.
11. In Fig.4C, co-localization of AKT1 and calreticulin should be quantitated.
12. In Fig. 4D, AKT1 levels in ER fractions were obviously lower in UFL1 knockdown ER fraction. However, in Fig. 4E,
AKT1 levels remained unchanged in UFL1 KD ER fractions. Please explain this discrepancy. Additionally, no increase of
AKT1 in cytoplasmic fractions was observed in UFL1 KD cells. Why?
13. In Fig.4F, more negative controls are needed.
14. in Fig.5A, please show the protein levels of shRNA-resistant AKT1s.
15. In Fig.6, it would be interesting to test the effect of UFL1(T426A) mutant on other UFM1 targets such as RPL26.
16. In Fig.7A and B, UFMylation inhibitor (Uba5 E1 inhibitor) DKM 2-93 dramatically reduced AKT1 UFMylation but had no
effect on overall UFMylation. Any explanation? Furthermore, if both inhibitors work through the route of AKT1, how was the
synergy achieved?
17. Please provide more experimental details, including antibody sources and RIDDs, web links, designs of shRNA
resistant genes, cell lines in each experiment, transient or stable lines, and etc.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Editor and Reviewers
Editor and Reviewers’ comments are highlighted in blue, and the response is provided below the
referee comments.
Reviewer #1 (AKT activation and posttranslational modifications, Remarks to the Author):
Summary:
This manuscript from Fei Meng et al presents a mechanistic study uncovering a positive feedback loop
between UFL1 and AKT1 in triple-negative breast cancer. The authors show that UFL1 promotes AKT1
activation through UFMylation at lysines K189, K276, and K297, facilitating AKT1’s ER localization
and interaction with upstream kinases PDK1 and mTORC2. In turn, AKT1 phosphorylates UFL1 at
T426, enhancing UFL1 activity and thereby amplifying UFMylation. This regulatory axis is shown to
control lipid metabolism and tumor growth, and the study further demonstrates that pharmacological
inhibition of UFMylation sensitizes cells to AKT inhibition and chemotherapy. These mechanistic
findings came from a comprehensive and rigorous experimental design, in which the authors combined
in vitro biochemistry, genetic models and in vivo xenograft mouse model. Moreover, the identification
and functional dissection of UFMylation (3K/R) and phosphorylation (T426) sites are well executed
and supported by multiple lines of evidence. The use of AKT and UFMylation inhibitors, and the
demonstration of synergy, provide a translational angle that strengthens the manuscript. Finally, the
emphasis on AKT1-mediated lipid accumulation connects this signaling axis to a well-established
hallmark of cancer. However, several key points need to be addressed to fully support the proposed
model.
Major Points for Revision:
1. Biochemical Evidence for AKT1 UFMylation in AKT activation: A key mechanistic claim of the
manuscript is that UFMylation of AKT1 at K189, K276, and K297 is required for its phosphorylation
at T308 and S473. However, in standard cellular models (including our own lab’s experience and
1
widely published studies), insulin or IGF-1 stimulation induces robust AKT1 phosphorylation without
any observable upward shift in AKT1 molecular weight on Western blot with the phospho-AKT1
specific antibodies. This raises an important question: if UFMylation were required for AKT
activation, why is the fully activated AKT with both p-T308 and p-S473 readily observed in the
absence of a UFM1-dependent band shift in these common settings? Please clarify whether the
proposed UFL1-AKT1 UFMylation axis is prior to AKT activation and whether the de-UFMylation of
fully activated AKT1 happened.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these constructive suggestions.
(1). Based on our findings that UFL1 depletion, UBA5 ablation, and mutation of AKT’s UFMylation
sites (3K/R) all significantly decreased AKT phosphorylation (Fig. 4A, B; Supplementary Fig. 4A-C
in the revised manuscript), we concluded that AKT UFMylation occurs prior to AKT phosphorylation.
(2). We agree that insulin or IGF-1-activated AKT1 displays no changes to its molecular weight, which
seems to conflict with the fact that UFMylation is required for AKT activation and UFM1’s molecular
weight is approximately 9 kDa. We hypothesized that AKT phosphorylation promotes its
deUFMylation. To address this, we performed the following experiments, and these results support
our prediction from different angles.
(i). Similar to other post-translational modifications, UFMylation is dynamic and reversible, and this
feature ensures that UFMylated AKT1 accounts for a tiny portion of total AKT1. Therefore,
endogenous AKT1 and p-S473 were examined using an anti-AKT1 antibody or an anti-p-S473 antibody
in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells with or without UFL1 depletion. After a long exposure,
weak p-S473 and AKT1 bands, whose molecular weights were approximately 27 kDa greater than that
of their corresponding lower bands due to UFMylation at K189, K276, and K297, were observed in
shSC cells, and these upper bands nearly disappeared in UFL1 knockdown cells (Supplementary Fig.
4K in the revised manuscript). Hence, a tiny amount of AKT1 is maintained in a UFMylation state,
perhaps due to deUFMylation.
2
[FIGURE REDACTED]
(ii). Covalently bound UFM1 is primarily cleaved from substrates by the cysteine protease UFSP2
(Christopher P. Walczak et al., 2019 PNAS. PMID: 30626644; Jessie Kulsuptrakul et al., 2021 Cell
Rep. PMID: 33730579)(Fig. 1 in this letter). Thus, UFSP2 was depleted by shRNA in MDA-MB-231
and MDA-MB-468 cells to assess whether inhibited deUFMylation leads to an increase in AKT1
UFMylation and an upward shift of the p-S473 band. As expected, the intensity of the upper p-S473
band and the UFMylated AKT1 band was both significantly increased in UFSP2 knockdown cells (Fig.
4H in the revised manuscript). These findings indicate that AKT1 undergoes deUFMylation.
(iii). p-T308 and p-S473 result in full AKT1 activation. A plasmid encoding a mutant AKT1 (referred
to as AKT1-DM), which harbors T308A and S473A mutations, was generated. MDA-MB-231 cells
expressing comparable levels of wild-type (AKT1-WT) and AKT1-DM were established. Compared
with AKT1-WT, AKT1-DM possessed higher levels of UFMylation (Fig. 4I in the revised manuscript),
suggesting that AKT1 phosphorylation enhances its deUFMylation.
(iv). Breast cancer cells expressing AKT1-WT and AKT1-DM were treated with or without insulin and
subjected to co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays. The interaction between UFSP2 and AKT1-WT
was stronger than the UFSP2-AKT1-DM association, and the former, but not the latter, interaction was
3
increased by insulin treatment (Fig. 4J in the revised manuscript). Hence, AKT1 phosphorylation
promotes the UFSP2-AKT1 interaction.
Collectively, these findings indicate that AKT1 UFMylation promotes AKT1 phosphorylation, which
in turn enhances the UFSP2-AKT1 interaction, thereby deUFMylating AKT1.
Notably, a similar phenomenon has been reported in AKT1 polyubiquitination (Wei-Lei Yang et al.,
C H Lin, S Y Liu, and E H Y Lee, 2016 Oncogene. PMID: 25867063), which significantly increase
AKT1’s molecular weight, while p-T308 and p-S473 bands with an upward shift are barely detectable.
Further investigations are needed to clarify whether ubiquitination, SUMOylation, and other post-
translational modifications of AKT1 are also removed by de-conjugation enzymes after AKT1 is
phosphorylated.
2. Breast cancer subtype specificity: While experiments include multiple breast cancer subtypes, the
core mechanistic and therapeutic data focus largely on TNBC cell lines. Some conclusions imply pan-
breast cancer relevance, but the experimental data supporting this are relatively limited. Please clarify
whether the UFL1-AKT1 feedback loop and its impact on lipid metabolism are broadly active across
subtypes, or primarily relevant in TNBC.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these valuable comments. The UFL1 mRNA and protein levels
are both increased in all breast cancer subtypes, including Luminal A, Luminal B, HER2+, and TNBC
(Supplementary Fig. 1A, D in the revised manuscript). UFL1 ablation suppressed the proliferation of
all breast cancer cell types (Fig. 1G, H; Supplementary Fig. 1E-G in the revised manuscript). All these
findings indicate that the UFL1-AKT1 feedback loop and its impact on lipid metabolism may be
broadly active across subtypes. To further test this hypothesis, we carried out the following
experiments:
(1). MCF-7 (Luminal A), BT474 (Luminal B), and SK-BR-3 (HER2+) cells were transfected with
vectors encoding AKT1-WT or AKT1-3K/R and subjected to UFMylation detection. Our results
4
indicated that AKT1-WT, but not AKT1-3K/R, was UFMylated in MCF-7, BT474, and SK-BR-3 cells
(Supplementary Fig. 3N-P in the revised manuscript), suggesting that K189, K276, and K297 are key
UFMylation sites in Luminal A, Luminal B, and HER2+ breast cancer cells. Additionally, we found
that AKT1-WT, but not AKT1-3K/R, enhanced lipid abundance in these breast cancer cells, as
evidenced by BODIPY staining assays (Supplementary Fig. 5H-M in the revised manuscript).
(2) MCF-7, BT474, and SK-BR-3 cells stably expressing UFL1-WT or UFL1-T426A were lysed for
UFL1 phosphorylation detection using an antibody that specifically recognizes phosphorylated UFL1
at T426 (referred to as p-UFL1 (T426) antibody). As expected, phosphorylation signals were only
observed in UFL1-WT, but not UFL1-T426A (Supplementary Fig. 6A in the revised manuscript). Thus,
p-UFL1 (T426) also occurs in Luminal A, Luminal B, and HER2+ breast cancer cells. Furthermore,
UFL1-WT increased lipid accumulation in MCF-7 and BT474 cells, whereas UFL1-T426A had no
impact on these cells (Supplementary Fig. 6G-J in the revised manuscript).
Taken together, these findings suggest that the UFL1-AKT1 feedback loop-mediated lipid metabolism
applies to all breast cancer subtypes. However, as we mentioned in the revised manuscript, TNBC is
more aggressive and lacks effective therapeutic targets; therefore, we mainly focused on TNBC in this
study.
3. Clinical relevance and correlation analysis: The manuscript refers to a positive correlation between
pUFL1 and pAKT1 in breast tumor tissues. However, the correlation coefficient (r) and significance
(p-value) are not clearly presented in the main text or figure legends. Please include the quantitative
data (r, p-value) and consider moving the correlation plot to a main figure to better support the clinical
relevance of the proposed axis.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these constructive suggestions. We quantitatively rescored the
specimens according to the percentage of immunopositive cells and the staining intensity, as
previously described (Ke Wu et al., 2023 Nat Cell Biol, PMID: 37156912). The sections were assigned
the following proportion scores: 0 if 0% of the tumor cells displayed positive staining, 1 for 0-1%, 2
5
for 2-10%, 3 for 11-30%, 4 for 31-70%, 5 for 71-100%. Additionally, the intensity of staining was
assigned a four-grade scale (0-3). Grades 0-3 represent: no expression (0), weak expression (1),
moderate expression (2), and strong expression (3). A total score (range, 0-8) was obtained by
combining the proportion and intensity scores. GraphPad Prism 8.0 was employed to perform the
Pearson correlation analysis (two-tailed). We have included these informations in the “Materials and
Methods” section of the revised manuscript. Additionally, as suggested, we have moved the correlation
plot from Supplementary Fig. 6 to Fig. 6T to better support the clinical relevance of the proposed axis,
and the correlation coefficient (r) and significance (p-value) have been presented in the Fig. 6T in the
revised manuscript.
4.Functional role of UFMylation beyond AKT1: The focus is tightly centered on AKT1, but the authors
note that other components of the lipid metabolism and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway may interact with
UFL1. Please comment more fully on whether UFMylation of othercomponents (e.g., ACLY, SREBP1
regulators) may contribute to the lipid phenotype, or whether this is uniquely AKT1-driven.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this recommendation. Rictor is a critical component of the
mTORC2 complex, and FASN catalyzes the conversion of Acetyl-CoA and Malonyl-CoA into long-
chain saturated fatty acids. Thus, they are essential for lipid synthesis. Our LC-MS/MS analysis
showed that Rictor and FASN are potential UFL1-interacting proteins (Supplementary Fig. 3A in the
revised manuscript). Co-IP and western blotting assays showed that UFL1 associates with and
UFMylates FASN and Rictor (Supplementary Fig. 3R-W in the revised manuscript). Moreover, UFL1
overexpression elevated lipid abundance, and this elevation was reversed by the FASN inhibitor C75
and Rictor inhibitor JR-AB2-011 (Supplementary Fig. 5O-T in the revised manuscript), suggesting that
UFL1 modulates lipid metabolism through multiple layers of mechanisms. Further investigations
should be performed to elucidate the mechanisms by which UFL1 controls FASN- and Rictor-mediated
lipid metabolism. The mass spectrometry raw data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange
Consortium via the PRIDE repository with the dataset identifier PXD062297. To access the dataset,
6
reviewers may log in to the PRIDE website using the username and password that have been submitted
to the editor.
Notably, AKT1 not only phosphorylates ACLY but also modulates the expression of multiple lipid
synthesis-related genes via SREBP1, therefore possessing a broad and profound impact on lipid
metabolism. Hence, we focused on the UFL1-AKT1 feedback loop, but not on FASN or Rictor in this
research.
Minor points:
1. Improve clarity in the Discussion to avoid repetition and to sharpen the distinction between known
and novel findings.
Response: Thank you for this suggestion. As suggested, we have rephrased the Discussion to avoid
repetition and to sharpen the distinction between known and novel findings in the revised manuscript.
2. Specify whether AKT2 and AKT3 were experimentally evaluated for UFMylation and ruled out
since it is surprisingly that UFL1 only targets AKT1 but negligible with AKT2 and 3.
Response: Thank you for your suggestion. AKT isoforms exhibit high sequence similarity, with
approximately 80% homology across the family, thereby possessing redundant functions. However,
AKT isoforms also possess unique or even opposing functions, suggesting that they may have different
regulators and downstream effectors. In this study, we found that the interaction between UFL1 and
AKT1 was stronger than the UFL1-AKT2 and UFL1-AKT3 associations (Supplementary Fig. 3C in the
revised manuscript). As suggested, we have detected the UFMylation of AKT2 and AKT3. The results
indicated that UFL1 also UFMylated AKT2 and AKT3, but their UFMylation was weaker than that of
AKT1 (Supplementary Fig. 3Q in the revised manuscript), probably due to their weak interaction with
UFL1. Collectively, these data demonstrate that AKT1 is the primary substrate of UFL1 in breast cancer
cells. The mechanism by which AKT isoforms display different binding affinity toward UFL1 should
be investigated in future studies.
7
3. Provide consistent cross-referencing between figures and legends, especially for
Supplementarydata.
Response: Thank you for your suggestion.We have carefully checked the cross-referencing between
figures and legends to ensure the consistency.
Reviewer #2 (Breast cancer and lipid metabolism, Remarks to the Author):
"The UFL1-AKT positive feedback loop promotes breast cancer progression by enhancing lipid
synthesis and drug resistance” by Meng, Du and Liang et al., nicely describes a new regulatory
mechanism of AKT based on UFMylation. The importance of UFMylation of AKT is supported by
convincing IP and in vivo rescue experiments. While the data supporting the posttranslational
modifications is convincing the more phenotypic data are unclear.
Main concerns:
1.The title: The title claims that UFL1-AKT feedback loop promotes breast cancer progression. There
is very little evidence that the pathway can actually drive the disease. There is a lot of evidence to
suggest that the pathway is required for progression. The only ectopic overexpression I could find was
lipid related in supp figure 2B-I. However, these do not include any in vivo or in vitro tumor outcome
data.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these constructive suggestions. To better support the conclusion
that the UFL1-AKT feedback loop promotes breast cancer progression, we performed experiments as
follows:
(1). Cell proliferation and BODIPY staining assays in vitro and xenograft assays in mice were
performed using parental and UFL1-overexpressed MDA-MB-231 or MDA-MB-468 breast cancer
cells (Fig. 2M-S; Supplementary Fig. 2D-R in the revised manuscript), and we found that UFL1
increased breast cancer cell proliferation and lipid accumulation in vitro (Supplementary Fig. 2D-N in
the revised manuscript) and breast tumor growth and lipids accumulation in vivo (Fig. 2M-S;
UFL1 was impaired by the SREBP1 inhibitor Fatostatin (Fig. 2M-S; Supplementary Fig. 2O-R in the
revised manuscript), which abolishes lipid synthesis. Together, these findings indicate that UFL1
functions as an oncogenic driver by modulating lipid synthesis in breast cancer.
(2). BODIPY staining assays indicated that AKT1-WT, but not AKT1-3K/R, enhanced lipid abundance
in MCF-7, BT474, and SK-BR-3 breast cancer cells, as evidenced by BODIPY staining assays
(Supplementary Fig. 5H-M in the revised manuscript). Moreover, AKT1-WT overexpression
significantly increased lipid abundance in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells (Supplementary Fig.
5O-T in the revised manuscript).
(3). BODIPY staining assays indicated that UFL1-WT increased lipid accumulation, whereas UFL1-
T426A had no effect in MCF-7 and BT474 breast cancer cells (Supplementary Fig. 6G-J in the revised
manuscript).
Collectively, these results suggest that the UFL1-AKT feedback loop promotes breast cancer
progression.
2. ER localization: The manuscript claims that UFL1 mediates an ER localization of AKT supported
by Immunofluorescence images (3F and 4C) and western blotting on cellular fractionation (4D). The
IF images should be shown at higher magnification, and the co-localization should be quantified. In
the same manner, the western blots should be repeated and quantified.
Response: We appreciate you raising these points. As suggested, the IF images have been shown at
higher magnification, and the co-localization has been quantified using the Fiji Colocalization Finder
plugin in ImageJ software (Fig. 3F; Supplementary Fig. 3D; Fig. 4C; and Supplementary Fig. 4D in
the revised manuscript). Meanwhile, repeated western blots in regular depletion studies, including Fig.
4A, 4D, 4H, 4K, 7C, and 7D, have been quantified (Supplementary Fig. 4A, E-H, L, N, O and
Supplementary Fig. 7A in the revised manuscript).
9
3. Western blot quantification: In general, western blots should be quantified where possible. I
understand this might be hard for some of the IP’s, but it should at the very least be done for regular
depletion studies as 4H. The figure legends consistently state at these blots have been repeated
independently three times. If so, please provide the quantification.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these suggestions. As suggested, repeated western blots in
regular depletion studies, including Fig. 4A, 4D, 4H, 4K, 7C, and 7D, have been quantified
(Supplementary Fig. 4A, E-H, L, N, O and Supplementary Fig. 7A in the revised manuscript).
4. Requirement of lipid synthesis: The requirement of lipid synthesis to be the driver of the UFL1
pathway needs more validation. Currently, the claim is backed by in vitro proliferation rescue with
OA (Supp 2J,K). Given the multitude of AKT effects on cancer cells, more conclusive evidence is
needed to back this claim.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these insightful suggestions. SREBP1 is the master transcription
factor that governs the expression of most rate-limiting enzymes involved in lipid synthesis. Thus,
SREBP1 depletion or inhibition is widely used for downregulating lipid accumulation. To strengthen
the conclusion that UFL1 exerts its oncogenic functions through lipid synthesis, we performed the
following experiments:
(1). Breast cancer cells stably expressing UFL1 were treated with or without the SREBP1 inhibitor
Fatostatin for subsequent lipid content measurement, BODIPY staining, and proliferation assays, and
the results showed that UFL1-induced lipid accumulation and proliferation were decreased by
Fatostatin (Supplementary Fig. 2D-N in the revised manuscript).
(2). Breast cancer cells harboring an empty vector (EV) or a vector encoding UFL1 were implanted
into the mammary fat pad of female NOD-SCID mice. When tumor volume reached approximately
200 mm3, Fatostatin was administered by intraperitoneal (IP) injection. In line with the in vitro results,
UFL1 promoted breast tumor growth and lipid accumulation in tumor tissues, and these phenotypes
10
were alleviated by Fatostatin (Fig. 2M-S and Supplementary Fig. 2O-R in the revised manuscript),
suggesting that UFL1 enhances tumor growth by modulating lipid synthesis.
(3). In cancer cells, lipid synthesis is remarkably enhanced to meet the demand for unlimited cell
proliferation and metastasis. Hence, increased lipid synthesis is a hallmark of breast cancer cells
(Miguel Martin-Perez et al., 2022 Cell Metab. PMID: 36261043; Felix C E Vogel, Adriano B Chaves-
Filho, and Almut Schulze, 2024 Nat Cancer. PMID: 38273023; Alexander R Terry and Nissim Hay,
but not AKT1-3K/R, enhanced lipid abundance in MCF-7, BT474, and SK-BR-3 breast cancer cells
(Supplementary Fig. 5H-M in the revised manuscript). Moreover, AKT1-WT overexpression
significantly increased lipid abundance in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells (Supplementary Fig.
5O-T in the revised manuscript).
(4) BODIPY staining assays indicated that UFL1-WT increased lipid accumulation, whereas UFL1-
T426A had no effect in MCF-7 and BT474 breast cancer cells (Supplementary Fig. 6G-J in the revised
manuscript).
Collectively, these results indicate that UFL1 exerts its oncogenic functions through enhancing lipid
synthesis.
Minor concerns:
1. All bar plots should display individual values.
Response: Thank you for your suggestions. As suggested, all bar plots now display individual data
points in the revised manuscript.
Line 110: In Figure 1E, I am guessing that the separation is based on the quantification in 1D. If so,
please relabel to low UFL1 and moderate/strong UFL1 (rather than simply high/low).
Response: Thank you for your suggestions. As suggested, “low UFL1” and “moderate/strong UFL1”
have been relabeled in Fig. 1E to maintain the consistency with Fig. 1D in the revised manuscript.
11
2. Line 111: Figure 1F. I believe this data is from the Tang data set, not Liu?
Response: Thank you for your reminder. The data were indeed from the Tang_2018 dataset, and we
have corrected this error in the revised manuscript.
3. Line 212: (data not shown). Please provide the data.
Response: Thank you for your suggestion. AKT isoforms exhibit high sequence similarity, with
approximately 80% homology across the family, thereby possessing redundant functions. However,
AKT isoforms also possess unique or even opposing functions, suggesting that they may have different
regulators and downstream effectors. In this study, we found that the interaction between UFL1 and
AKT1 was stronger than the UFL1-AKT2 and UFL1-AKT3 associations (SupplementaryFig. 3C in the
revised manuscript). As suggested, we have detected the UFMylation of AKT2 and AKT3. The results
indicated that UFL1 also UFMylated AKT2 and AKT3, but their UFMylation was weaker than that of
AKT1 (SupplementaryFig. 3Q in the revised manuscript), probably due to their weak interaction with
UFL1. Collectively, these data demonstrate that AKT1 is the primary substrate of UFL1 in breast cancer
cells. The mechanism by which AKT isoforms display different binding affinity toward UFL1 should
be investigated in future studies. As suggested, we have included these data in Supplementary Fig.
3Q in the revised manuscript.
4. Line 498: Why are the cells treated with 1mM sodium citrate for 12 hours before staining for Bodipy
and oil red O? And how does that impact the measurements? I am guessing citrate will boost the acetyl-
CoA levels and thus possibly the lipid synthesis. However, the citrate incubation is not typically
required to identify lipid droplets. Does the data hold up without the preincubation?
Response: Thank you for your questions. Except for liver cells, the intensity of BODIPY and Oil Red
O (ORO) staining in most other cell types, including cancer cells, is very low. For example, the ORO
and BODIPY signals are very weak in MDA-MB-231, MDA-MB-468, and MCF-7 cells (Heather J
Wright et al., 2017 PNAS. PMID: 28739932; Yangjing Zhao et al., 2022 Adv Sci. PMID: 34747157;
Jiamin Lin et al., 2023 eLife. PMID: 38078907) (Fig. 2A, B; Fig. 3A; and Fig. 5A in this letter).
and BODIPY signals (Yanjie Tan et al., 2024 Nat Commun. PMID: 39333556; Jiamin Lin et al., 2023
eLife. PMID: 38078907) (Fig. 3 and Fig. 5A in this letter). However, low dose OA (100 or 200 μM)
can dramatically increase the ability of breast cancer cells to proliferate and invade (Jiamin Lin et al.,
2023 eLife. PMID: 38078907) (Fig. 5A-D in this letter). In contrast, 1 mM sodium citrate (SCT)
significantly increases lipid droplet accumulation (Yangjing Zhao et al., 2022 Adv Sci. PMID:
34747157) (Fig. 4A in this letter) without affecting breast cancer cell proliferation and apoptosis
(Yangjing Zhao et al., 2022 Adv Sci. PMID: 34747157) (Fig. 4B, C in this letter). Therefore, we utilized
1 mM SCT to enhance the ORO and BODIPY signals in this study.
To rule out the possibility that 1 mM SCT affects our conclusion, we compared the intensity of
BODIPY staining in shSC and shUFL1#1 MDA-MB-231 cells in the presence or absence of 1 mM SCT.
We found that 1 mM SCT markedly increased BODIPY signals, and UFL1 depletion significantly
decreased BODIPY signals with or without SCT treatment (Fig. 6 in this letter). This is rational,
because UFL1 activates AKT, thereby enhancing the activity of ACLY, which catalyzes the conversion
of citrate into Acetyl-CoA. Thus, 1 mM SCT treatment does not change our conclusion that UFL1 is
[FIGURE REDACTED]
13
essential for lipid accumulation. These results are non-essential for this study; therefore, we have
provided them here for your review.
The manuscript by Meng et al reported the critical role of the UFL1-AKT axis in breast cancer
progression and drug resistance. Specifically, the authors found that AKT1 was UFMylated by UFL1,
an UFMylation-specific E3 ligase, in breast cancer cells. AKT1 UFMylation promoted its ER
recruitment and activation by both PDK1 and mTORC2, which in turn enhanced lipid biogenesis and
cancer progression. Moreover, the authors showed that AKT1 phosphorylated UFL1 and boosted
UFL1’s activity. Finally, UFL1 expression was elevated in breast cancer samples and associated with
poor prognosis in human patients. Targeting both UFMylation and AKT1 had a synergetic effect on
TNBC in xenograft models.
Overall, the finding of the positive feed-back regulation between AKT1 and UFL1 appears to be novel
and may represent a potential target for cancer therapy. However, there are some significant flaws in
data analysis and interpretation that should be addressed. As described below, this reviewer failed to
duplicate some of the results as claimed by the authors regarding the association between UFL1 mRNA
level and overall survival of human BC patients. In addition, a few pieces of experimental data
appeared to conflict to each other, and some results were difficult to explain. Finally, the evidence to
support the role of lipid metabolism in tumor progression is relatively insufficient.
Specific comments:
1. Concerns on bioinformatic analyses of BC databases and clinical samples.
a. This reviewer failed to duplicate KM survival curves using GEPIA database (http://gepia.cancer-
pku.cn). A simple search using UFL1 and BRCA dataset in GEPIA yielded no significant association
between Ufl1 mRNA levels and overall survival of BC patients. The number of patients also differed
from what the authors reported.
into High and Low expression groups. When the High and Low expression groups are denoted as
Cutoff-High (50%) and Cutoff-Low (50%), the numbers of the High and Low groups are 535 and 533,
respectively. Thus, the total number of samples is 1068 (Fig. 7A in this letter). In fact, the KM analysis
was performed by assigning the high and low expression groups with Cutoff-High (22%) and Cutoff-
Low (78%), respectively. Thus, the number of the High group and the Low group should be 235
(1068*22%) and 833 (1068*78%), respectively (Fig. 7B in this letter). However, the numbers of the
High group and Low group were both incorrectly labeled as 835 on the GEPIA website, and we
overlooked correcting them in the initial submission. This error has been corrected in Fig. 1B in the
revised manuscript.
b. In Fig.S1C, GSE9693 dataset was about “Clostridioides difficile”, which was nothing to do with
breast cancer.
Response: Thank you for your reminder. GSE9693 is a typo; it should be GSE9893 (Fig. 8A in this
letter). We have corrected this error in Supplementary Fig. 1C in the revised manuscript.
c. In Fig. 1F, this reviewer could not replicate the KM survival plot as reported using KM plotter
database (kmplot.com). There was no reference or GSE number for Liu-2014 dataset (as indicated in
Fig. 1F). Additionally, none of BC datasets in KMplot could generate similar survival plots showing
16
the significant correlation between Ufl1 mRNA level and overall survival. Please provide more
information on the dateset and UFL1 (named as KIAA0776 in KM plot) probe set used in the analysis
reported by the authors.
Response: Thank you for your reminder. The data were derived from the Tang_2018 dataset (Fig. 8B
in this letter), and we have corrected this copy-and-paste error in Fig. 1F in the revised manuscript.
2. Specificity of Ufl1 antibody in IHC. The authors did not provide the source of UFL1 and other
antibodies. To the knowledge of this reviewer, some commercial UFL1 antibodies recognized multiple
bands in immunoblotting. Even though Fig.1K may have indirectly addressed this issue, more stringent
test should be done to examine the specificity of UFL1 antibody. Meanwhile, the knockdown efficiency
of UFL1 shRNAs should be shown.
Response: Thank you for your reminder.
(1). We have provided the catalog number and RRID of all antibodies in the “Materials and Methods”
section of the revised manuscript.
(2). Anti-UFL1 antibody (HPA030559, RRID: AB_10600537) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich,
and the specificity of this antibody has been confirmed in vitro and in vivo in multiple published papers,
such as Nat Cell Biol (Jiang Liu et al., PMID: 32807901), Adv Sci (Jiongjie Jing et al., PMID:
39985286), and PNAS (Junzhi Zhou et al., PMID: 36893266). To further examine the specificity of
this anti-UFL1 antibody, we are providing the whole WB membranes of UFL1 in shSC and shUFL1
breast cancer cells. These membranes indicate that this antibody specifically recognizes UFL1 bands
17
(Fig. 9 in this letter), and the UFL1 knockdown efficiency is very high (Fig. 9in this letter; Fig. 1G, H
and Supplementary Fig. 1E-G in the revised manuscript). Moreover, the IHC staining in Fig. 1K in the
revised manuscript also validates the specificity of this anti-UFL1 antibody. Since the specificity of
the UFL1 antibody has been verified in published papers, we will not include the whole WB
membranes of UFL1 in shSC and shUFL1 breast cancer cells in the revised manuscript. Instead, we
have provided them here for your review.
3. For cell death assay of tissue culture cells, Annexin V staining or TUNEL should be done in addition
to CC3 staining.
Response: Thank you for your suggestion. As suggested, Annexin-V and propidium iodide (PI)
staining have been performed for flow cytometry assays (Supplementary Fig. 1L, M in the revised
manuscript), and the results were consistent with those from CC3 staining.
4. The claim that UFL1 is an oncogenic driver (Fig.1) appears to be an overstatement. Even though
UFL1 overexpression promoted cell proliferation, no experimental evidence supported its oncogenic
activity.
Response: Thank you for these constructive suggestions. To better support the conclusion that UFL1
promotes breast cancer progression, we performed experiments as follows:
(1). Cell proliferation and BODIPY staining assays in vitro and xenograft assays in mice were
performed using parental and UFL1-overexpressed MDA-MB-231 or MDA-MB-468 breast cancer
cells (Fig. 2M-S and Supplementary Fig. 2D-R in the revised manuscript), and we found that UFL1
increased breast cancer cell proliferation and lipid accumulation in vitro (Supplementary Fig. 2D-N
18
and Supplementary Fig. 5O-T in the revised manuscript) and breast tumor growth and lipid
accumulation in vivo (Fig. 2M-S and Supplementary Fig. 2O-R in the revised manuscript).
Interestingly, the cancer-promoting effect of UFL1 was impaired by the SREBP1 inhibitor Fatostatin
(Fig. 2M-S and Supplementary Fig. 2O-R in the revised manuscript), which abolishes lipid synthesis.
Together, these findings indicate that UFL1 functions as an oncogenic driver by modulating lipid
abundance in breast cancer.
(2). BODIPY staining assays indicated that AKT1-WT, but not AKT1-3K/R, enhanced lipid abundance
in MCF-7, BT474, and SK-BR-3 breast cancer cells, as evidenced by BODIPY staining assays
(Supplementary Fig. 5H-M in the revised manuscript). Hence, UFL1 enhances lipid accumulation in a
UFMylation-dependent manner.
Collectively, these results suggest that UFL1 promotes breast cancer progression via modulation of
lipid synthesis.
5. The claim that UFL1 promotes breast cancer cell growth by increasing lipid accumulation was
backed up by the only functional assay that was shown in Fig.S2J and K, in which addition of OA
reversed UFL1 knockdown phenotype. Since lipid metabolism was such a big part of this study, more
functional experiments should be done to firmly establish the relationship between lipid metabolism,
the UFL1-AKT axis and tumor progression.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these constructive suggestions. SREBP1 is the master
transcription factor that governs the expression of most rate-limiting enzymes involved in lipid
synthesis. Thus, SREBP1 depletion or inhibition is widely used for downregulating lipid accumulation.
To strengthen the conclusion that UFL1 exerts its oncogenic functions through lipid synthesis, we
performed the following experiments:
(1). Breast cancer cells stably expressing UFL1 were treated with or without the SREBP1 inhibitor
Fatostatin for subsequent lipid content measurement, BODIPY staining, and proliferation assays, and
the results showed that UFL1-induced lipid accumulation and proliferation were decreased by
Fatostatin (Supplementary Fig. 2D-N in the revised manuscript).
(2). Breast cancer cells harboring an empty vector (EV) or a vector encoding UFL1 were implanted
into the mammary fat pad of female NOD-SCID mice. When tumor volume reached approximately
200 mm3, Fatostatin was administered by intraperitoneal (IP) injection. In line with the in vitro results,
UFL1 promoted breast tumor growth and lipid accumulation in tumor tissues, and these phenotypes
were alleviated by Fatostatin (Fig. 2M-S and Supplementary Fig. 2O-R in the revised manuscript),
suggesting that UFL1 enhances tumor growth by modulating lipid synthesis.
(3). In cancer cells, lipid synthesis is remarkably enhanced to meet the demand for unlimited cell
proliferation and metastasis. Hence, increased lipid synthesis is a hallmark of breast cancer cells
(Miguel Martin-Perez et al., 2022 Cell Metab. PMID: 36261043; Felix C E Vogel, Adriano B Chaves-
Filho, and Almut Schulze, 2024 Nat Cancer. PMID: 38273023; Alexander R Terry and Nissim Hay,
but not AKT1-3K/R, enhanced lipid abundance in MCF-7, BT474, and SK-BR-3 breast cancer cells,
as evidenced by BODIPY staining assays (Supplementary Fig. 5H-M in the revised manuscript).
Moreover, AKT1-WT overexpression significantly increased lipid abundance in MDA-MB-231 and
MDA-MB-468 cells (Supplementary Fig. 5O-T in the revised manuscript).
(4). BODIPY staining assays indicated that UFL1-WT increased lipid accumulation, whereas UFL1-
T426A had no effect in MCF-7 and BT474 breast cancer cells (Supplementary Fig. 6G-J in the revised
manuscript).
Collectively, these results indicate that UFL1 exerts its oncogenic functions through enhancing lipid
synthesis.
6. High-quality of confocal imaging in Fig.3F should be provided. The current one appeared to be
fuzzy, especially UFL1.
high-quality confocal images, the colocalization of UFL1 and AKT1 was quantified using the Fiji
Colocalization Finder plugin in ImageJ software (Fig. 3F and Supplementary Fig. 3D in the revised
manuscript), and selected regions were magnified to improve the visual effect.
7. As shown in Fig.3I and J, knockdown of UFL1 led to reduced AKT UFMylation but had no effect
on overall UFMylation (especially RPL26 UFMylation, around 27kD and higher), a result that seems
to contradict to previous studies. Please explain why.
Response: Thank you for your reminder. Overall UFMylation was not affected by UFL1 ablation,
which may be due to two reasons: the specific lysis buffer for UFMylation detection was not fresh
enough, and too much protein was loaded for UFM1 detection. To avoid these problems mentioned
above, we repeated all these assays using the following fresh lysis buffer: HEK293T or breast cancer
cells were collected and resuspended in a buffer containing 150 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 5% sodium
dodecyl sulfate (SDS), and 30% glycerol, followed by boiling for 10 minutes. Cell lysates were diluted
with buffer A (50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% NP-40, 2 mM N-ethylmaleimide, and
protease inhibitors) at a 1:20 ratio and incubated with the indicated antibodies and protein A/G
magnetic beads (Bio-Rad) at 4 °C overnight. The immunoprecipitates were boiled in 1 x Laemmli
buffer, separated by SDS-PAGE, and analyzed by WB. For overall UFMylation (UFM1) detection, 5-
10 μg of whole cell lysates were loaded. In this case, a reduction in overall UFMylation was observed
upon UFL1 ablation (Fig. 3I, J in the revised manuscript) and UFMylation inhibitor treatment (Fig. 7A,
B in the revised manuscript). Notably, UFL1 overexpression only had a minimal impact on overall
UFMylation (Supplementary Fig. 3I, J in the revised manuscript) probably due to high levels and
activity of endogenous UFL1 in breast cancer cells (Fig. 1C, D; Supplementary Fig. 1D; Fig. 6T; and
Supplementary Fig. 6M in the revised manuscript).
8. In Fig.3I and J and other similar figures, please provide the results of IgGs as negative controls in
those IPs.
negative controls in Fig. 3I, J, L, M; Supplementary Fig 3I, J, N-Q; Fig. 4F, G, I; Supplementary Fig.
4J; Supplementary Fig. 6B; and Fig. 7A, B in the revised manuscript.
9. In Fig.3, it was showed that UFM1 antibody could detect UFMylated endogenous and exogenous
AKT1. How about AKT1 and Flag antibodies?
Response: Thank you for your valuable suggestions. Similar to other post-translational modifications,
UFMylation is dynamic and reversible, and this feature ensures that UFMylated AKT1 accounts for a
tiny portion of total AKT1. Therefore, endogenous AKT1 was examined using an anti-AKT1 antibody
in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells with or without UFL1 depletion. After a long exposure,
two AKT1 bands were observed in the parental cells (Supplementary Fig. 4K in the revised manuscript).
The molecular weight of the upper AKT1 (UFMylated AKT1) bands was approximately 27 kDa greater
than that of their corresponding lower bands, and the upper bands were very weak (Supplementary
Fig. 4K in the revised manuscript). These upper bands nearly disappeared in UFL1 knockdown cells
(Supplementary Fig. 4K in the revised manuscript). In contrast, UFL1 overexpression significantly
increased the intensity of upper Flag-AKT1 (UFMylated Flag-AKT1) in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-
MB-468 cells (Fig. 10 in this letter). Covalently bound UFM1 is primarily cleaved from substrates by
the cysteine protease UFSP2 (Christopher P. Walczak et al., 2019 PNAS. PMID: 30626644; Jessie
Kulsuptrakul et al., 2021 Cell Rep. PMID: 33730579) (Fig. 1 in this letter). Thus, UFSP2 was depleted
by shRNA in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells to assess whether inhibited deUFMylation leads
to an increase in AKT1 UFMylation and an upward shift of the AKT1 band. As expected, the intensity
of the UFMylated AKT1 bands was significantly increased in UFSP2 knockdown cells (Fig. 4H in the
revised manuscript).
22
10. In Fig. 4A and B, it would be interesting to examine if phosphorylation of other mTORC2 and
PDK1 targets is altered by UFL1 knockdown.
Response: Thank you for your suggestions. PKCα and PLK1 are well-known targets of mTORC2
(Timothy R Baffi et al., 2021 Sci Signal. PMID: 33850054; Tsuneo Ikenoue et al., 2008 EMBO J.
PMID: 18566587) and PDK1 (Jing Tan et al., 2013 Cancer Discov. PMID: 23887393), respectively.
Hence, we determined the phosphorylation of PKCα and PLK1 in shSC and shUFL1 MDA-MB-231
and MDA-MB-468 cellsand found that UFL1 depletion significantly downregulated the protein levels
of phosphorylated PKCα but had no impact on PLK1 phosphorylation (Supplementary Fig. 4M in the
revised manuscript). It is reasonable that UFL1 affected PKCα phosphorylation because UFL1
interacted with and UFMylated Rictor, which is a critical component of the mTORC2 complex
(Supplementary Fig. 3T, U, W in the revised manuscript).
11. In Fig.4C, co-localization of AKT1 and calreticulin should be quantitated.
Response: Thank you for your suggestions. As suggested, the colocalization of AKT1 and calreticulin
has been quantified using the Fiji Colocalization Finder plugin in ImageJ software (Supplementary
Fig. 4D in the revised manuscript).
12. In Fig. 4D, AKT1 levels in ER fractions were obviously lower in UFL1 knockdown ER fraction.
However, in Fig. 4E, AKT1 levels remained unchanged in UFL1 KD ER fractions. Please explain this
discrepancy. Additionally, no increase of AKT1 in cytoplasmic fractions was observed in UFL1 KD
cells. Why?
Response: Thank you for your reminder. This discrepancy may be caused by excess loading of protein
lysate. After reducing protein loading, decreased AKT1 levels in ER fractions were observed (Fig. 4D
in the revised manuscript). In quiescent cells, AKT1 predominantly localizes in the cytosol. Growth
factors and other stimuli stimulate PH domain-dependent accumulation of AKT1 at the respective
membranes. AKT1 membrane accumulation is transient, typically peaking around 2-5 min after
stimulation (Véronique Calleja et al., 2007 PloS Biol. PMID: 17407381; Michael Ebner et al., 2017 Mol
(Hiroyuki Kubota 2012 Mol Cell. PMID: 22633957; Michael Ebner et al., 2017 Mol Cell. PMID:
28157504). This observation, among others, has led to the prevailing model of Akt signaling, whereby
it is activated at the membrane but dissociates from the membrane and freely diffuses in the cytosol in
a “locked” active state, phosphorylating its numerous substrates (Corina E Antal and Alexandra C
Newton, 2013 Mol Cell Proteomics. PMID: 23788531; Véronique Calleja et al., 2007 PloS Biol. PMID:
17407381; Véronique Calleja, Michel Laguerre, and Banafshé Larijani, 2009 J Chem Biol. PMID:
19568789; R Meier et al., 1997 J Biol Chem. PMID: 9374542). From this perspective, all inactive AKT1
and most active AKT1 exist in the cytosol, and the influence of UFL1 depletion on the AKT1 levels in
the cytoplasmic fraction is negligible. In contrast, UFL1 depletion dramatically affected p-T308 and p-
S473 levels in both the cytosol and ER membrane.
13. In Fig.4F, more negative controls are needed.
Response: Thank you for your suggestions. As suggested, we have provided the results of IgG as a
negative control in those immunoprecipitation experiments (Fig. 4F in the revised manuscript).
14. in Fig.5A, please show the protein levels of shRNA-resistant AKT1s.
Response: Thank you for your suggestions. AKT1 was knocked down by shAKT1
(CGTGCCATGATCTGTATTTAA) targeting its 3’UTR. Therefore, shAKT1 only depletes
endogenous AKT1, without affecting ectopically expressed AKT1. We have included this information
in the “Materials and Methods” section of the revised manuscript and presented the protein levels of
AKT1 in shSC, shAKT1, shAKT1+AKT1-WT, and shAKT1+AKT1-3K/R in Supplementary Fig. 5A in
the revised manuscript.
15. In Fig.6, it would be interesting to test the effect of UFL1 (T426A) mutant on other UFM1 targets
such as RPL26.
Response: Thank you for your suggestions. The protein levels of total RPL26 (Supplementary Fig.
6B in the revised manuscript) and UFMylated RPL26 (as indicated by asterisks in Supplementary Fig.
24
6B in the revised manuscript) were both comparable in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells
expressing UFL1-WT and UFL1-T426A, suggesting that p-UFL1 (T426) may specifically modulate
the AKT signaling pathway. Notably, AMPK phosphorylates UFL1 at T536, disrupting the UFL1-PD1
interaction and PD1 UFMylation to trigger its degradation in T cells (Chuan He et al., 2024 Mol Cell.
PMID: 38377992). Upon DNA damage, ATM phosphorylates UFL1 at S462 to enhance its ligase
activity and promote ATM activation in a positive feedback loop, thereby facilitating DNA damage
repair (Bo Qin et al., 2019 Nat Commun. PMID: 30886146). Thus, UFL1 phosphorylation at distinct
amino acids may dictate substrate specificity, ultimately determining its biological function.
16. In Fig.7A and B, UFMylation inhibitor (Uba5 E1 inhibitor) DKM 2-93 dramatically reduced AKT1
UFMylation but had no effect on overall UFMylation. Any explanation? Furthermore, if both
inhibitors work through the route of AKT1, how was the synergy achieved?
Response: Thank you for your constructive questions.
(1). Similar to your question #7, overall UFMylation was not affected by UBA5 and AKT inhibitors,
which may be due to two reasons: the specific lysis buffer for UFMylation detection was not fresh
enough, and too much protein was loaded for UFM1 detection. To avoid these problems, we repeated
all these assays using the following fresh lysis buffer: HEK293T or breast cancer cells were collected
and resuspended in a buffer containing 150 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 5% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS),
and 30% glycerol, followed by boiling for 10 minutes.Cell lysates were diluted with buffer A (50 mM
Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% NP-40, 2 mM N-ethylmaleimide, and protease inhibitors) at a
1:20 ratio and incubated with the indicated antibodies and protein A/G magnetic beads (Bio-Rad) at
4 °C overnight. The immunoprecipitates were boiled in 1 x Laemmli buffer, separated by SDS-PAGE,
and analyzed by WB. For overall UFMylation (UFM1) detection, 5-10 μg of whole cell lysates were
loaded. In this case, a reduction in overall UFMylation was observed upon UFMylation inhibitor
treatment (Fig. 7A, B in the revised manuscript). Notably, UFL1 overexpression only had a minimal
impact on overall UFMylation (Supplementary Fig. 3I, J in the revised manuscript) probably due to
25
high levels and activity of endogenous UFL1 in breast cancer cells (Fig. 1C, D, Supplementary Fig. 1D;
Fig. 6T, Supplementary Fig. 6M in the revised manuscript).
(2). Synergistic combinations of two or more agents can overcome toxicity and other side effects
associated with high doses of single drugs by countering biological compensation, allowing reduced
dosage of each compound or accessing context-specific multitarget mechanisms (Joseph Lehár et al.,
Rev Cancer. PMID: 38627557). Multiple promising combinatorial strategies have been developed to
achieve synergistic effects, such as vertical inhibition, disruption of positive feedback loops, blocking
parallel signaling pathways, and preventing compensatory bypass signaling. ① Vertical inhibition
consists of inhibiting the main oncogenic driver, which is genetically altered, often mutated or
amplified, together with an upstream or downstream component of the same oncogenic pathway, to
achieve a deeper suppression of the pathway (Naiara Perurena, Lisa Situ, and Karen Cichowski, 2024
Nat Rev Cancer. PMID: 38627557; David Shahbazian, Joshua Sznol, and Harriet M Kluger, 2012 Adv
Pharmacol. PMID: 22959021). From this perspective, AKT1 is the main oncogenic driver, UFL1 (or
other components of the UFMylation system) is an upstream component of the AKT1 pathway; the
combination of an AKT1 inhibitor and a UBA5 inhibitor achieved a deeper suppression of the AKT1
pathway (Fig. 7 in the revised manuscript). Thus, the combination of an AKT1 inhibitor and a UBA5
inhibitor constitutes a vertical inhibition. Similarly, PDK1 phosphorylates AKT1 at T308, and a PDK1
inhibitor (GSK2334470) and an AKT1 inhibitor (Ipatasertib and MK-2206) achieve a synergistic effect
(Emily K Slotkin et al., 2019 Cancer Discov. PMID: 30877085; Kristyna Kupcova et al., 2024 Exp
Hematol Oncol. PMID: 39487517). PRMT5 methylates and subsequently activates AKT1, and a
PRMT5 inhibitor (GSK3326595) and an AKT inhibitor (MK-2206) display a synergistic effect on
promoting cell death (Shasha Yin et al., 2021 Nat Commun. PMID: 34103528). ② When Protein A
and Protein B directly or indirectly activate each other (forming a positive feedback loop), their
inhibitors frequently exhibit strong synergistic effects. This occurs because blocking either protein
26
alone leaves the other free to reactivate its partner, while dual inhibition almost collapses the entire
signaling circuit (Joseph Lehár et al., 2009 Nat Biotechnol. PMID: 19581876;Deborah Plana, Adam C
Palmer, and Peter K Sorger, 2022 Cancer Discov. PMID: 34983746). In this regard, AKT1 and UFL1
reciprocally activate each other to form a positive feedback loop; therefore, their inhibitors exert a
synergistic anti-cancer effect. In the same manner, an AKT inhibitor (MK-2206) and an mTOR
inhibitor (Everolimus) (Yvonne Yeung et al., 2017 Mol Oncol. PMID: 28544747), an EGFR inhibitor
(Gefitinib) and a MEK inhibitor (Trametinib) (João M Fernandes Neto et al., 2020 Nat Commun.
PMID: 32572029), and a STAT3 inhibitor (Napabucasin) and an IL-6 inhibitor (Tocilizumab) (Anibal
Méndez-Clemente et al., 2022 Oncol Rep. PMID: 35703345) exhibit synergistic anti-cancer effects. In
summary, the UBA5 inhibitor sensitizes breast cancer cells to the AKT1 inhibitor, and their
combination achieves a deeper suppression of AKT1 signaling and breast tumor growth, thereby
exhibiting a synergistic effect.
17. Please provide more experimental details, including antibody sources and RIDDs, web links,
designs of shRNA resistant genes, cell lines in each experiment, transient or stable lines, and etc.
Response: Thank you for your reminder. (1) We have provided the catalog numbers, RRIDs, and
sources of antibodies in the “Materials and Methods” section of the revised manuscript. (2) We have
provided the web links of Sigma-Aldrich Advanced Genomics, PrimerBank, Gene Expression
Profiling Interactive Analysis (GEPIA), Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), ProteomeXchange
Consortium, PRoteomics IDEntifications Database (PRIDE), and Kaplan-Meier plotter in the
“Materials and Methods” and “Data Availability” sections of the revised manuscript. (3) UFL1 and
AKT1 were depleted by shUFL1#1 (GGAACTTGTTAATAGCGGA) and shAKT1
(CGTGCCATGATCTGTATTTAA) targeting their 3’UTR, respectively. Therefore, shUFL1#1 and
shAKT1 only knockdown endogenous UFL1 and AKT1, without affecting exogenous cDNAs of UFL1
and AKT1. We have included this information in the “Materials and Methods” section of the revised
27
manuscript. (4) As suggested, the information regarding cell lines and transient or stable lines has been
included in the revised manuscript.
28

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This manuscript from Fei Meng et al. presents a mechanistic study defining a positive feedback loop
between UFL1 and AKT1 in breast cancer. The authors demonstrate that UFL1 UFMylates AKT1 at
lysines K189, K276, and K297, promoting its ER localization and phosphorylation by PDK1 and
mTORC2. In turn, AKT1 phosphorylates UFL1 at T426, enhancing UFL1 ligase activity and
reinforcing AKT1 UFMylation. This reciprocal regulation drives lipid accumulation and tumor growth,
while pharmacological inhibition of UFMylation synergizes with AKT inhibition and sensitizes cells
to chemotherapy.
In this revised manuscript, the authors have convincingly addressed the previous concerns by
providing additional biochemical evidence for the dynamic nature of AKT1 UFMylation and de-
UFMylation. The authors extended their analyses to multiple breast cancer subtypes, incorporating
quantitative clinical correlation data, and broadened their discussion of UFMylation substrates beyond
AKT1. The new experiments, including UFSP2 knockdown, AKT1 phosphorylation-deficient mutants,
and expanded xenograft and lipid metabolism assays, strengthen the mechanistic model and enhance
clinical relevance.
Overall, the study is comprehensive, rigorous, and meaningful. The mechanistic dissection of
UFMylation and phosphorylation sites is well handled, and the therapeutic angle is compelling. This
work significantly improves upon the initial version and now provides strong support for the proposed
UFL1–AKT1 feedback loop as a driver of lipid metabolism and tumor growth in breast cancer.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

UFMylation, a ubiquitin-like modification, is crucial for cellular processes and is linked to human diseases, including cancer. However, its role in cancer remains unclear. Here, we report that UFL1 promotes breast tumor growth by remodeling lipid metabolism. Mechanistically, UFL1 interacts with and UFMylates AKT, enhancing its localization at the endoplasmic reticulum and phosphorylation by PDK1 and mTORC2, thereby increasing AKT-mediated lipid synthesis. Moreover, AKT phosphorylates UFL1, boosting its activity. Thus, UFL1 and AKT form a positive feedback loop, accelerating lipid synthesis and breast tumor growth. Clinically, UFL1 levels are increased in human breast tumors and are associated with poor clinical outcomes in breast cancer patients. Importantly, UFMylation inhibitors sensitize breast cancer cells to AKT inhibitors and anticancer drugs. Our findings reveal a critical role for UFMylation in lipid metabolism and identify the UFL1-AKT axis as a potential therapeutic target in breast cancer.

## Introduction

UFMylation, a ubiquitin-like modification, is sequentially catalyzed by E1 (UBA5, ubiquitin-like modifier activating enzyme 5), E2 (UFC1, ubiquitin-fold modifier-conjugating enzyme 1), and E3 (UFL1, UFM1-specific ligase 1), leading to the covalent conjugation of ubiquitin-fold modifier 1 (UFM1) to the lysine residues of substrates1–3. Currently, UFL1 is the sole E3 ligase for UFMylation; however, by itself, UFL1 is unstable and inactive4,5. UFBP1 (UFM1 binding protein 1) is essential for UFL1 stability and activity1,6,7. UFMylation is a highly dynamic process, and UFM1 can be removed from UFMylated substrates by UFSP1/2 (UFM1-specific proteases 1/2) to prevent excessive UFMylation8–10. A growing body of evidence highlights the functional importance of UFMylation in various biological processes, such as DNA damage repair11–14 and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress response15,16. Although UFMylation dysregulation has been implicated in cancers, only a few UFMylation substrates have been identified in cancer cells, and the functions and molecular mechanisms of UFMylation in cancer remain largely uncharted. Moreover, UFMylation exhibits different, or even opposing, functions depending on cancer types or subtypes17. Therefore, identifying novel UFMylation substrates and deciphering their functions, as well as the underlying mechanisms, will advance our understanding of the fundamental roles of UFMylation in cancer and may potentially benefit cancer treatment. Recent research shows that UFL1 depletion in bovine mammary epithelial cells dramatically decreases the expression of lipid synthesis-related genes, while UFBP1 ablation increases lipid accumulation in hepatocytes18,19, suggesting potential roles for UFMylation in lipid metabolism under physiological conditions, although the underlying mechanisms remain elusive. However, whether and how UFMylation modulates lipid metabolism in cancer remains to be explored.

Increased de novo lipid synthesis contributes to the unlimited proliferation and survival of cancer cells and is therefore considered a hallmark of cancer20,21. The serine/threonine protein kinase AKT (also known as protein kinase B, PKB) plays a central role in de novo lipogenesis by directly regulating the activity of ACLY (ATP citrate lyase) or indirectly modulating the expression of ACC1 (acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1), FASN (fatty acid synthase), ACSS2 (acyl-CoA synthetase short-chain family member 2), SCD1 (stearoyl-CoA desaturase), and HMGCR (3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA reductase), which are rate-limiting enzymes in de novo lipid synthesis22,23. In mammalian cells, there are three AKT isoforms (AKT1, AKT2, and AKT3), which possess redundant as well as unique functions23. AKT1 is an oncogenic kinase that is hyperphosphorylated and overactive in most human cancers24, with elevated AKT1 activity observed in approximately 40% of breast cancers25. The recruitment of AKT1 to the plasma membrane or intracellular membrane through binding of its PH (pleckstrin homology) domain to PIP3 (phosphatidylinositol 3,4,5-trisphosphate) is a prerequisite for AKT1 phosphorylation at threonine (T) 308 by PDK1 and at serine (S) 473 by Rictor-mTOR complex (mTORC2)26,27. Phosphorylation at T308 and S473 leads to full AKT1 activation26. Despite reports that ubiquitination28, methylation29,30, and SUMOylation31 control AKT1 activity, the mechanisms underlying AKT1 membrane localization and activity remain poorly understood.

In the present study, we report that a positive feedback loop between UFL1 and AKT1 promotes breast tumor growth by reprogramming lipid metabolism. Mechanistically, UFL1 UFMylates AKT1 at lysines (K) 189, K276, and K297, disrupting the interaction between the PH domain and KD (kinase domain) of AKT1, thereby facilitating AKT1 localization at the ER and subsequent phosphorylation at T308 and S473 by PDK1 and mTORC2, respectively. Interestingly, AKT1 phosphorylation stimulates UFSP2-mediated AKT1 deUFMylation. On the other hand, AKT1 phosphorylates UFL1 at T426, enhancing UFL1 activity and AKT1 UFMylation by UFL1. Activated AKT1 sustains breast tumor growth by phosphorylating ACLY and inducing the expression of several lipogenic genes to reinforce lipid synthesis. Clinically, the mRNA and protein levels of UFL1 are both elevated in breast cancer tissues and negatively correlate with the overall survival of breast cancer patients. Intriguingly, the levels of phosphorylated UFL1 and phosphorylated AKT1 display a positive correlation in human breast tumors. Importantly, targeting UFMylation and AKT1 exhibits a synergistic anticancer effect in vitro and in vivo. Our findings delineate a mechanism in lipid metabolism via the UFL1-AKT1 positive feedback loop and uncover this regulatory loop as a potential therapeutic target in breast cancer.
