## Results

UFL1 possesses oncogenic potential in breast cancer
UFL1 is the only E3 ligase in the UFMylation system, but its expression and function in cancers are highly context-dependent. Previous studies on UFL1 in breast cancer, even within the same breast cancer subtype, have led to controversial conclusions32,33. To comprehensively evaluate the clinical relevance of UFL1, we first assessed its expression levels in human breast tumors. Analysis of the Gene Expression Profiling Interactive Analysis (GEPIA) breast cancer dataset revealed that UFL1 mRNA levels were significantly increased in human breast tumors compared with normal breast tissues (Fig. 1A). This elevation was observed in all breast cancer subtypes, including Luminal A, Luminal B, human epidermal growth factor receptor 2-positive (HER2+), and triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) (Supplementary Fig. 1A). The Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) dataset also indicated the highest levels of UFL1 mRNA in stage III breast cancers (Supplementary Fig. 1B). Importantly, GEPIA (Fig. 1B) and GEO (Supplementary Fig. 1C) datasets both showed that high levels of UFL1 mRNA were associated with decreased overall survival in breast cancer patients. Furthermore, we performed immunohistochemistry (IHC) assays and found that UFL1 protein levels were markedly upregulated in breast tumors (Fig. 1C, D), and all breast cancer subtypes showed elevated UFL1 protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 1D). Consistently, moderate and high levels of UFL1 protein were associated with poor clinical outcomes in breast cancer patients (Fig. 1E). A similar negative correlation was found in the Kaplan–Meier Plotter dataset (Fig. 1F). Collectively, UFL1 expression is increased in breast tumors and negatively correlates with clinical outcomes in breast cancer patients.

The aforementioned findings prompted us to hypothesize that UFL1 is an oncogenic protein in breast cancer. To confirm this hypothesis, UFL1 was depleted in MCF-7 (Luminal A), BT474 (Luminal B), SK-BR-3 (HER2+), MDA-MB-231 (TNBC), and MDA-MB-468 (TNBC) breast cancer cells using two independent shRNAs targeting UFL1 (shUFL1#1 and shUFL1#2) for cell growth assays. Compared with scrambled shRNA (shSC), shUFL1#1 and shUFL1#2 dramatically suppressed breast cancer cell growth (Fig. 1G, H; Supplementary Fig. 1E–G). Due to the lack of effective therapeutic targets, TNBC is much more aggressive than other breast cancer subtypes. Therefore, we mainly focused on TNBC cells. Cell growth is coordinately controlled by cell proliferation and cell death. Immunostaining assays showed that UFL1 depletion dramatically downregulated Ki-67 (a cell proliferation marker) protein levels (Supplementary Fig. 1H, I), while increasing the protein levels of cleaved caspase-3 (CC3, a cell death marker) (Supplementary Fig. 1J, K). Consistently, the intensity of Annexin-V (a marker of early apoptotic cells) and propidium iodide (PI, a marker of necrotic or late apoptotic cells) staining was significantly increased by UFL1 ablation, as evidenced by flow cytometry assays (Supplementary Fig. 1L, M). All these results suggested a critical role for UFL1 in promoting proliferation and suppressing cell death. Next, we conducted xenograft mouse assays. shSC, shUFL1#1, and shUFL1#2 MDA-MB-468 cells were implanted into the mammary fat pads of female NOD-SCID mice. As expected, UFL1 depletion significantly inhibited MDA-MB-468 tumor growth (Fig. 1I, J; Supplementary Fig. 1N). Consistently, immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining revealed that UFL1 knockdown markedly enhanced cell death and impeded cell proliferation, as evidenced by increased CC3-positive cell numbers and decreased Ki-67-positive cell numbers, respectively (Fig. 1K–N). Taken together, these findings indicate that UFL1 promotes breast tumor growth by increasing cell proliferation and repressing cell death.

UFL1 is indispensable for lipid accumulation in breast cancer cells
To delineate the mechanism of UFL1-mediated breast tumor growth, we conducted Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) using the Biomarker Exploration for Solid Tumors (BEST, https://rookieutopia.com/) database to identify biological processes potentially regulated by UFL1 in breast cancer34. Fatty acid metabolism emerged as a strong candidate (Supplementary Fig. 2A), as lipid synthesis and lipid accumulation are usually elevated in cancer cells and positively correlate with poor clinical outcomes35–37. Additionally, previous studies have shown that dysfunction of the UFMylation system alters lipid accumulation, although the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood18,19. Based on these findings, we hypothesized that UFL1 may modulate lipid metabolism in breast cancer cells. To test this hypothesis, we analyzed lipid content by performing Oil Red O (ORO) staining and ORO absorbance assays in UFL1 knockdown TNBC cells38. As expected, the absorbance of eluted ORO at 510 nm was significantly downregulated by UFL1 ablation in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells (Fig. 2A, B). Furthermore, we quantified lipid content using the fluorescent lipid dye BODIPY 493/503. Consistent with the ORO staining results, UFL1 depletion significantly decreased lipid accumulation, as evidenced by decreased BODIPY 493/503 fluorescence intensity in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells (Fig. 2C–F). In accordance with these findings, the levels of total free fatty acids and cholesterol were both decreased by UFL1 ablation in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells (Fig. 2G–J). Importantly, lipid abundance in MDA-MB-468 breast tumors was markedly decreased by UFL1 knockdown (Fig. 2K, L). Taken together, these results demonstrate that UFL1 regulates lipid accumulation in breast cancer cells.

To confirm whether UFL1 controls breast cancer cell growth by modulating lipid accumulation, control and UFL1 knockdown breast cancer cells were cultured in low-serum medium (1% FBS) for 24 h and subsequently incubated with or without oleic acid (OA), one of the most abundant fatty acids that promote breast cancer cell proliferation at low concentration39. Our results showed that the decreased growth of breast cancer cells due to UFL1 depletion was almost completely restored by OA supplementation (Supplementary Fig. 2B, C), indicating that UFL1 promotes breast cancer cell growth by elevating lipid abundance. SREBP1 controls the expression of several rate-limiting enzymes involved in lipid synthesis, including ACLY, ACC1, SCD1, and FASN40. Therefore, MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells stably expressing UFL1 were established (Supplementary Fig. 2D) and cultured in the presence or absence of the SREBP1 inhibitor Fatostatin. As expected, UFL1 overexpression significantly increased the levels of total free fatty acids and cholesterol, and this increase was almost completely abolished by Fatostatin (Supplementary Fig. 2E–H), suggesting that UFL1 may modulate lipid synthesis in breast cancer cells. This conclusion was well supported by the results of BODIPY 493/503 staining assays (Supplementary Fig. 2I–L). Importantly, UFL1 overexpression-induced cell proliferation was diminished by Fatostatin treatment (Supplementary Fig. 2M, N). Collectively, these data indicate that UFL1 promotes breast cancer cell growth by increasing lipid synthesis.

To further validate the prediction that UFL1 exerts its oncogenic functions through modulating lipid accumulation in vivo, xenograft assays were performed by injecting MDA-MB-231 cells harboring an empty vector (EV) or a vector encoding UFL1 into the mammary fat pads of female NOD-SCID mice, followed by intraperitoneal (IP) injection of vehicle or Fatostatin. In keeping with the in vitro findings, ectopically expressed UFL1 promoted breast tumor growth (Fig. 2M, N; Supplementary Fig. 2O), increased lipid abundance (Fig. 2O, P), suppressed cell death (Fig. 2Q, R), and enhanced cell proliferation (Fig. 2Q, S), without affecting the body weight of tumor-bearing mice (Supplementary Fig. 2P). These effects of UFL1 in breast tumors were effectively reversed by Fatostatin (Fig. 2M–S; Supplementary Fig. 2O–R). Taken together, these results demonstrate that UFL1 promotes breast tumor growth by regulating lipid synthesis.

UFL1 interacts with and UFMylates AKT
To elucidate the mechanism of UFL1-mediated lipid accumulation, we performed liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) assays using MDA-MB-231 cells stably expressing Flag-UFL1 to identify potential substrates of UFL1. LC-MS/MS analysis revealed that AKT1 is a high-confidence potential UFL1-binding protein (Supplementary Fig. 3A). Notably, several key components of the UFMylation system, such as DDRGK1 (UFBP1), CDK5RAP3, UFM1 and UFC1, as well as more than 10 well-known UFL1 substrates, including PARP114, RPL2616, MRE1112, 13 and p5341, were also identified in the list of putative UFL1-interacting proteins (Supplementary Fig. 3A), confirming the feasibility of our approach. Moreover, GSEA analysis via the BEST database indicated that UFL1 may regulate the PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling pathway, which is critical for lipid metabolism (Supplementary Fig. 3B). Consistent with the LC-MS/MS analysis, exogenous UFL1 showed a robust interaction with ectopically expressed AKT1 but weakly associated with AKT1’s paralogs, AKT2 or AKT3, in HEK293T cells (Supplementary Fig. 3C). Hence, we focused on AKT1. The endogenous interaction between UFL1 and AKT1 was also observed in MDA-MB-231 (Fig. 3A, B) and MDA-MB-468 (Fig. 3C, D) cells. To further determine whether UFL1 directly binds to AKT1, we performed in vitro GST pull-down assays using purified GST-AKT1 and immunoprecipitated UFL1 from breast cancer cells. UFL1 was pulled down by GST-AKT1 but not by GST alone (Fig. 3E), suggesting a direct interaction between UFL1 and AKT1. Given that UFL1 predominantly localizes to the perinuclear ER6,7, we performed immunofluorescence staining and found that UFL1 and AKT1 mainly colocalized at the perinuclear region of MDA-MB-231 cells (Fig. 3F; Supplementary Fig. 3D), suggesting potential ER colocalization of UFL1 and AKT1 in breast cancer cells. Next, we sought to identify the domains that mediate the UFL1-AKT1 interaction. Domain-mapping assays indicated that UFL1 associates with AKT1 via its N-terminus (Fig. 3G, H; Supplementary Fig. 3E, F). Additionally, AKT1 associated with UFBP1 and UFC1 (Supplementary Fig. 3G, H), suggesting that UFL1 may modulate AKT1 in a UFMylation-dependent manner.

Indeed, AKT1 was UFMylated in breast cancer cells, and this modification was significantly decreased by UFL1 ablation in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells (Fig. 3I, J). In contrast, ectopic expression of UFL1 in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells led to upregulation of AKT1 UFMylation (Supplementary Fig. 3I, J). UFL1 is inactive on its own and is activated by forming a complex with UFBP15,42,43. Mutation of leucine (L) 45 to arginine (R) in UFL1 (L45R) disrupts the UFL1-UFBP1 interaction5,42,43. To further assess the impact of UFL1 activation on AKT1 UFMylation, we compared the effect of wild-type (WT) and L45R mutant UFL1 and found that only WT UFL1, not L45R UFL1, was capable of UFMylating AKT1 (Supplementary Fig. 3K). These data confirm that UFL1 UFMylates AKT1 in breast cancer cells. To identify potential UFMylation sites in AKT1, we assessed UFMylation within AKT1’s conserved domains, including the PH domain, KD, and CD (C-terminal domain). Our results showed that UFMylation levels were significantly higher in the KD compared to the PH domain and CD (Fig. 3K), suggesting that the primary UFMylation sites are located within the KD. The KD contains six conserved lysine (K) residues (Supplementary Fig. 3L), and we constructed Flag-AKT1 variants with single mutations at each of these K residues to assess UFMylation in HEK293T cells. Notably, single mutations of K to R at positions K189, K276, or K297 significantly reduced AKT1 UFMylation (Supplementary Fig. 3M), indicating that these sites are key for AKT1 UFMylation. Indeed, a triple mutation of these residues (referred to as 3K/R) nearly abolished AKT1 UFMylation (Supplementary Fig. 3M). To further confirm that AKT1 is UFMylated at K189, K276, and K297 in TNBC cells, we expressed both WT and 3K/R mutant Flag-AKT1 at comparable levels in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells. Compared with Flag-AKT1-WT, the UFMylation levels of Flag-AKT1-3K/R were significantly lower in these TNBC cells (Fig. 3L, M). Similar results were obtained from MCF-7, BT474, and SK-BR-3 breast cancer cells (Supplementary Fig. 3N–P). These findings demonstrate that K189, K276, and K297 are key UFMylation sites in AKT1 in breast cancer cells. Although K189, K276, and K297 are conserved in AKT2 and AKT3, their UFMylation levels were lower than those in AKT1 (Supplementary Fig. 3Q) potentially due to their weak association with UFL1 (Supplementary Fig. 3C), suggesting that AKT1 is the primary substrate of UFL1. Intriguingly, other lipid synthetic enzymes, such as FASN and Rictor (Supplementary Fig. 3A), were also identified as potential UFL1-interacting proteins in LC-MS/MS analysis, prompting us to test their UFMylation. Indeed, UFL1 associated with and UFMylated FASN and Rictor in breast cancer cells (Supplementary Fig. 3R–W). Compared with FASN and Rictor, AKT1 possesses a much more comprehensive and profound impact on lipid synthesis, Hence, we focused on AKT1. Collectively, our data demonstrate that UFL1 directly associates with AKT1 and UFMylates AKT1 at K189, K276, and K297 in breast cancer cells.

AKT UFMylation is a prerequisite for AKT activation and AKT-mediated lipid synthesis
UFMylation regulates protein stability or activity6,7, prompting us to assess its impact on AKT1 protein levels and AKT1 phosphorylation at T308 (p-AKT1(T308)) and S473 (p-AKT1(S473)), both of which are critical for AKT1 activation and function. Remarkably, we observed a reduction in p-AKT1(T308) and p-AKT1(S473) in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells upon UFL1 depletion, while the AKT1 protein levels remained unchanged (Fig. 4A; Supplementary Fig. 4A). Similar results were obtained in MCF-7, SK-BR-3, and BT474 cells (Supplementary Fig. 4B). In line with these findings, depletion of UBA5, the unique E1 enzyme of the UFMylation system, led to decreased AKT1 phosphorylation (Supplementary Fig. 4C). Thus, AKT1 UFMylation regulates its phosphorylation without affecting its stability. Moreover, when MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells expressing comparable levels of Flag-AKT1-WT and Flag-AKT1-3K/R were analyzed for phosphorylation, Flag-AKT1-WT showed robust phosphorylation at T308 and S473, whereas p-AKT1(T308) and p-AKT1(S473) were nearly undetectable in Flag-AKT1-3K/R (Fig. 4B). These results indicate that UFMylation at K189, K276, and K297 is essential for AKT1 phosphorylation and full activation.

It has been suggested that AKT1 membrane localization and the disruption of AKT1 autoinhibition are critical for its full activation, but the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood44–51. As mentioned above, UFL1 is a perinuclear ER-resident protein that colocalizes with AKT1 in the perinuclear region of breast cancer cells (Fig. 3F), suggesting that UFL1 may influence AKT1’s ER localization. Consistent with this hypothesis, our immunostaining experiments showed that UFL1 knockdown significantly impaired the colocalization of AKT1 with the well-known ER marker Calreticulin (Fig. 4C; Supplementary Fig. 4D). Furthermore, subcellular fractionation assays revealed that the abundance of AKT1, p-AKT1(T308), and p-AKT1(S473) on the ER was decreased by UFL1 depletion in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells, regardless of insulin treatment, which induces PIP3 generation (Fig. 4D; Supplementary Fig. 4E–H). By contrast, the protein levels of p-AKT1(T308) and p-AKT1(S473), but not AKT1, were reduced in the cytosol following UFL1 ablation (Fig. 4D; Supplementary Fig. 4E–H). In contrast, UFL1 overexpression enhanced AKT1 ER localization and activation in MDA-MB-231 cells (Supplementary Fig. 4I). Moreover, PIP3-conjugated beads were used for co-IP assays with lysates of ER fractions isolated from control and UFL1 knockdown breast cancer cells, with or without insulin treatment. UFL1 depletion markedly reduced the association between AKT1 and PIP3 on the ER (Fig. 4E). These findings suggest that UFL1 promotes AKT1 ER localization and activation. Intramolecular interaction between the PH domain and KD maintains AKT1 in an inactive state46,52–54. Notably, AKT1-3K/R mutation remarkably strengthened the interaction between the PH domain and KD in breast cancer cells (Fig. 4F), indicating that AKT1 UFMylation triggers a conformation change in AKT1, thereby abolishing AKT1 autoinhibition. Taken together, UFL1 enhances AKT1 ER localization, relieves AKT1 autoinhibition, and consequently triggers AKT1 activation in breast cancer cells.

PDK1 and mTORC2 are responsible for the phosphorylation of AKT1 at T308 and S473, respectively55,56. We predicted that UFL1 might influence the interaction between AKT1 and mTORC2 or PDK1. As shown in Fig. 4G, the endogenous interactions of AKT1 with Rictor and PDK1 were both dramatically mitigated by UFL1 knockdown in TNBC cells. Conversely, UFL1 overexpression enhanced the interaction of AKT1 with Rictor and PDK1 in TNBC cells (Supplementary Fig. 4J). Notably, neither depletion nor overexpression of UFL1 influenced the protein levels of PDK1 and Rictor (Fig. 4G; Supplementary Fig. 4J). These findings suggest that UFL1 strengthens the interaction between AKT1 and Rictor, as well as between AKT1 and PDK1, in breast cancer cells. It is worth noting that UFMylation seemed to have no impact on the molecular weight of phosphorylated AKT1, suggesting that AKT1 phosphorylation may promote its deUFMylation. To verify this prediction, endogenous AKT1 and phosphorylated AKT1(S473) were examined by western blotting analysis using an anti-AKT1 antibody or an anti-p-AKT1(S473) antibody. After a long exposure, weak p-S473 and AKT1 bands, whose molecular weights were approximately 27 kDa greater than that of their corresponding lower bands, were observed in shSC cells, and these upper bands nearly disappeared in UFL1 knockdown cells (Supplementary Fig. 4K). On the contrary, the intensity of the upper bands was robustly increased by depletion of UFSP2 (Fig. 4H; Supplementary Fig. 4L), which catalyzes deUFMylation. These data indicated that phosphorylated AKT1 may undergo deUFMylation. Indeed, the UFMylation levels of AKT1-WT were much lower than those of mutant AKT1 (AKT1-DM), which harbors T308A and S473A mutations (Fig. 4I). Moreover, the interaction between UFSP2 and AKT1-WT was stronger than the UFSP2-AKT1-DM association, and the former, but not the latter, interaction was increased by insulin treatment (Fig. 4J). Notably, UFL1 depletion also downregulated the protein levels of phosphorylated but not total PLK1 (Supplementary Fig. 4M), which is a substrate of mTORC2, probably due to UFL1-dependent Rictor UFMylation (Supplementary Fig. 3T, U, W). In contrast, UFL1 ablation did not influence total and phosphorylated PKCα (Supplementary Fig. 4M), which is a substrate of PDK1. These results indicated that UFL1 may modulate mTORC2 activity by UFMylating Rictor. Taken together, UFMylation promotes PDK1- and mTORC2-mediated AKT1 phosphorylation, which in turn accelerates UFSP2-mediated AKT1 deUFMylation.

Active AKT1 is essential for de novo lipid synthesis through the phosphorylation of ACLY and activation of SREBP1, a transcription factor that drives the transcription of several genes involved in lipid synthesis, including ACLY, ACC1, SCD1, and FASN40. UFL1 depletion significantly decreased the protein levels of phosphorylated ACLY (p-ACLY (S455)), although the total ACLY protein levels were slightly reduced (Fig. 4K; Supplementary Fig. 4N, O). Additionally, the protein levels of ACC1, ACSL3, and FASN were also downregulated by UFL1 knockdown, likely due to impaired SREBP1 maturation (Fig. 4K; Supplementary Fig. 4N, O). In contrast, UFL1 overexpression elevated the levels of p-ACLY (S455), ACLY, ACSL3, ACC1, and FASN (Supplementary Fig. 4P). Consistently, UFL1 ablation suppressed the mRNA levels of these lipid synthesis-related genes (Supplementary Fig. 4Q), without perturbing the transcription of genes involved in lipid export (Supplementary Fig. 4R), uptake (Supplementary Fig. 4S), or oxidation (Supplementary Fig. 4T). Collectively, these results indicate that UFL1 promotes AKT1-mediated ACLY phosphorylation and the transcription of lipid synthesis-related genes, thereby enhancing lipid synthesis and accumulation.

Deficiency in AKT UFMylation impairs its oncogenic potential
Since AKT1 activation is impaired in the absence of AKT1 UFMylation, we hypothesized that AKT1-mediated lipid accumulation and breast tumor growth would be attenuated by the 3K/R mutation. Indeed, ORO and BODIPY 493/503 staining assays showed that the decreased lipid accumulation due to AKT1 ablation was completely restored by AKT1-WT, but not AKT1-3K/R, in TNBC cells (Fig. 5A–D; Supplementary Fig. 5A–E). In line with these findings, the reduction in free fatty acids and cholesterol abundance due to AKT1 depletion was rescued by AKT1-WT, but not by the AKT1-3K/R, in TNBC cells (Fig. 5E, F; Supplementary Fig. 5F, G). Additionally, overexpressed AKT1-WT, but not AKT1-3K/R, elevated lipid abundance in MCF-7, BT474, and SK-BR-3 cells (Supplementary Fig. 5H–M). Hence, UFL1 promotes lipid accumulation through UFMylated AKT1. To explore the role of AKT1 UFMylation in tumorigenesis in vivo, we conducted xenograft mouse assays. As expected, the retarded growth of MDA-MB-231 breast tumors caused by AKT1 ablation was restored by AKT1-WT, but the 3K/R mutant AKT1 failed to do so (Fig. 5G, H; Supplementary Fig. 5N). Consistent with the results in Fig. 5A–F, the disturbed lipid accumulation caused by AKT1 knockdown in breast tumors was rescued by AKT1-WT, but not by AKT1-3K/R, as evidenced by ORO staining (Fig. 5I, J). IHC staining indicated that AKT1 depletion in MDA-MB-231 tumors led to increased CC3 and decreased Ki-67 signals, which were reversed by reconstituted AKT1-WT, but not by AKT1-3K/R (Fig. 5K–M). These findings suggest that AKT1 UFMylation plays a critical role in regulating cell proliferation and cell death in breast tumors. Importantly, AKT1-WT, but not AKT1-3K/R, in shAKT1 breast tumors displayed comparable levels of p-AKT1(T308) and p-AKT1(S473) to those observed in shSC control tumors (Fig. 5K, N–P). This indicates that AKT1 UFMylation is essential for AKT1 phosphorylation and activation in breast tumors. Given that UFL1 also UFMylates FASN and Rictor, we further evaluated lipid abundance in UFL1-overexpressed breast cancer cells treated with or without the FASN inhibitor C75 or the Rictor inhibitor JR-AB2-011. Unsurprisingly, increased lipid accumulation by ectopic UFL1 was dramatically ameliorated by C75 and JR-AB2-011 (Supplementary Fig. 5O–T), suggesting that UFL1 also controls lipid accumulation via FASN and Rictor. Taken together, our results highlight that AKT1 UFMylation is crucial for AKT1’s oncogenic functions, both in vitro and in vivo.

UFL1 phosphorylation by AKT is required for UFL1-mediated breast tumor growth
Given that AKT1 interacts with UFL1, which possesses a canonical AKT consensus phosphorylation motif (Fig. 6A), we speculated that AKT1 might phosphorylate UFL1. Indeed, immunoblotting using a commercial antibody that specifically recognizes phosphorylated AKT substrates (referred to as p-AKT-sub) indicated that UFL1 was phosphorylated in MDA-MB-231 cells, and this phosphorylation was enhanced by insulin, which activates AKT1 (Fig. 6B). More importantly, AKT1 depletion completely abolished this p-AKT-sub signal (Fig. 6B). The in vitro kinase assay demonstrated that Flag-UFL1 immunoprecipitated from MDA-MB-231 cells was phosphorylated by purified GST-AKT1, but not by GST alone (Fig. 6C). These results establish UFL1 as an AKT1 substrate in breast cancer cells. To determine whether T426 in UFL1 was the phosphorylation site targeted by AKT1, WT and T426A mutant Flag-UFL1 were stably expressed alone or in combination with Myc-AKT1 in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells, followed by immunoblotting with a specific antibody for T426 phosphorylation (referred to as p-UFL1(T426)). The p-UFL1(T426) signal was observed in UFL1-WT, but not in UFL1-T426A (Fig. 6D, E). Similar results were observed in MCF-7, SK-BR-3, and BT474 breast cancer cells (Supplementary Fig. 6A). Thus, AKT1 phosphorylates UFL1 at T426 in breast cancer cells. Since UFL1 modulates AKT1 activation, we next examined whether p-UFL1(T426) affects AKT1 UFMylation and phosphorylation. As expected, UFL1-WT, but not UFL1-T426A, increased AKT1 UFMylation (Supplementary Fig. 6B), as well as p-AKT1(T308) and p-AKT1(S473) (Fig. 6F, G), in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells, suggesting that phosphorylation is critical for UFL1 activity. Notably, T426A mutation had no impact on total and UFMylated RPL26 (Supplementary Fig. 6B), indicating that p-UFL1(T426) may specifically modulate AKT signaling. Together, these results indicate that AKT1 and UFL1 form a positive feedback loop to mutually enhance their activities.

The above finding prompted us to investigate the impact of p-UFL1(T426) on UFL1-mediated lipid accumulation and tumorigenesis. To this end, we first assessed lipid abundance in breast cancer cells using ORO and BODIPY 493/503 staining. Our results showed that the reduction in lipid abundance due to UFL1 depletion was restored by UFL1-WT, but not by UFL1-T426A, in both MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells (Fig. 6H–K; Supplementary Fig. 6C–F). Moreover, UFL1-WT, but not UFL1-T426A, elevated lipid accumulation in MCF-7 and BT474 cells (Supplementary Fig. 6G–J). Next, we performed xenograft mouse assays with mammary fat pad injections. The inhibitory effect of shUFL1#1 on MDA-MB-231 breast tumor growth and lipid abundance in the tumors was completely reversed by WT, but not T426A, UFL1 (Fig. 6L–O; Supplementary Fig. 6K). IHC analysis further revealed that UFL1’s ability to promote cell proliferation and suppress cell death was significantly impaired by the T426A mutation (Fig. 6P, Q; Supplementary Fig. 6L). Notably, the T426A mutation also abolished p-UFL1(T426) signal in breast tumors, compared to UFL1-WT (Fig. 6R, S; Supplementary Fig. 6L). Intriguingly, the levels of p-UFL1(T426) and p-AKT1(S473) exhibited a positive correlation in TNBC tissues (Fig. 6T; Supplementary Fig. 6M), suggesting a rationale for the combination of UFMylation and AKT1 inhibition in breast cancer treatment. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that p-UFL1 (T426), mediated by AKT1, is essential for UFL1 to control lipid accumulation and drive breast tumor growth.

UFMylation inhibitors synergize with AKT inhibitors in breast cancer treatment
Although several ongoing clinical trials are investigating AKT inhibitors in advanced solid tumors, the clinical benefits of these AKT inhibitors have been limited due to their low efficacy, non-selectivity, and the development of resistance57,58, necessitating a combination of AKT inhibitors with other chemotherapies. UFMylation inhibitor DKM 2-93 and AKT inhibitor MK-2206 both significantly decreased AKT1 UFMylation and phosphorylation (Fig. 7A–D). Co-treatment with DKM 2-93 and MK-2206 displayed a synergistic inhibitory effect on AKT1 UFMylation (Fig. 7A, B), AKT1 phosphorylation (Fig. 7C, D; Supplementary Fig. 7A), and lipid accumulation (Fig. 7E–H; Supplementary Fig. 7B–E) in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells. Consistently, DKM 2-93 and MK-2206 synergistically inhibited the viability of these breast cancer cells (Supplementary Fig. 7F, G). Activated AKT1 has been reported to alleviate the sensitivity of breast cancer cells to clinical drugs, including cisplatin and etoposide59. Since DKM 2-93 markedly suppresses AKT1 activation, we examined whether DKM 2-93 could sensitize breast cancer cells to these chemotherapeutic agents. As expected, DKM 2-93 sensitized MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 breast cancer cells to both cisplatin and etoposide (Supplementary Fig. 7H–K). Furthermore, in breast tumor-bearing mice treated with DKM 2-93 and MK-2206, we observed a significant reduction in tumor volume and lipid abundance compared to tumors treated with DKM 2-93 or MK-2206 alone (Fig. 7I–K, M; Supplementary Fig. 7L). Of note, the body weights of the mice remained identical (Supplementary Fig. 7M). Similarly, the combination of DKM 2-93 and MK-2206 synergistically suppressed p-AKT1(S473) (Fig. 7L, N), p-UFL1(T426) (Fig. 7L, O), and cell proliferation (Fig. 7L, P), while promoting cell death (Fig. 7L, Q) in the tumors. Notably, DKM 2-93 and MK-2206 did not alter the protein levels of AKT or UFL1 (Supplementary Fig. 7N, Q). In summary, targeting AKT1 UFMylation represents a promising strategy for sensitizing breast cancer cells to AKT inhibitors or chemotherapeutic agents.

## Methods

Cell culture
MDA-MB-231, MDA-MB-468, MCF-7, SK-BR-3, BT474, and HEK293T cells were obtained from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) and cultured in DMEM (CM15019, Macgene), RPMI 1640 (Macgene, CM10041), or McCoy’s 5A (Macgene, CM10051) medium, supplemented with 10% FBS (ExCell, FSP500), 1% penicillin, and 1% streptomycin. All cells were confirmed to be mycoplasma-free and cultured at 37 °C with 5% CO2.

Plasmids
Full-length and truncated cDNAs of human UFL1, UFBP1, UFM1, UFC1, AKT1, AKT2, and AKT3 were PCR-amplified and subsequently cloned into lentiviral vectors, including pLVX-IRES-Flag, pLVX-IRES-HA, and pLVX-IRES-Myc. For protein purification, full-length and truncated AKT1 were subcloned into the pGEX-6P-1 vector. Site-directed mutagenesis was employed to generate mutant UFL1 and AKT1. The shRNA sequences targeting human UFL1 (shRNA#1 targets 3’UTR: GGAACTTGTTAATAGCGGA; shRNA#2 targets CDS: GAGGAGTAATTTTTACGGA), AKT1 (shAKT1 targets 3’UTR: CGTGCCATGATCTGTATTTAA), UBA5 (shUBA5 targets CDS: CCTCAGTGTGATGACAGAAAT), and UFSP2 (shUFSP2#1 targets CDS: GACTGATGCTTCTGCTTGTAA; shUFSP2#2 targets CDS: GCTGAAGACCTGCAAGTTATT) were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich Advanced Genomics (https://www.sigmaaldrich.cn/CN/en/products/molecular-biology-and-functional-genomics/gene-editing-and-functional-genomics#products) and subsequently incorporated into the pLKO.1 lentiviral vector. Additional plasmids used in this study have been described in previous publications63. All constructs were verified through DNA sequencing. Plasmid transfection was conducted using PolyJet (SignaGen, SL100688) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Lentivirus production and establishment of stable cell lines
Lentivirus was generated as described previously64. Briefly, HEK293T cells were co-transfected with individual expression plasmids and the packaging vectors pMD2.G and psPAX2 using PolyJet (SignaGen, SL100688) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Forty-eight hours post-transfection, virus particles were harvested and filtered using a 0.45 μm syringe filter. Breast cancer cells were co-cultured with the lentivirus for 48 h, followed by selection with puromycin (1.0 μg/mL, Abcam, ab141453) or G418 (3 mg/mL, MedChemExpress, HY-17561) for an additional 4–8 days. All knockdown and overexpression breast cancer cell lines are stable.

Antibody
Anti-Flag antibody (20543-1-AP; RRID: AB_11232216; 1:8000 for WB (western blotting)), anti-Flag antibody (66008-4-Ig; RRID: AB_2918475; 1:8000 for WB), anti-HA antibody (51064-2-AP; RRID: AB_11042321; 1:5000 for WB), anti-Myc antibody (16286-1-AP; RRID: AB_11182162; 1:5000 for WB), anti-Myc antibody (60003-2-Ig; RRID: AB_2734122; 1:5000 for WB), anti-β-actin antibody (66009-1-Ig; RRID: AB_2687938; 1:10000 for WB), anti-GAPDH antibody (10494-1-AP; RRID: AB_2263076; 1:10000 for WB), anti-Rictor antibody (27248-1-AP; RRID: AB_2880817; 1:1000 for WB), anti-ACC1 antibody (21923-1-AP; RRID: AB_11042445; 1:1000 for WB), anti-ACLY antibody (15421-1-AP; RRID: AB_2223741; 1:1000 for WB), anti-ACSL3 antibody (20710-1-AP; RRID: AB_10697670; 1:1000 for WB), anti-FASN antibody (10624-2-AP; RRID: AB_2100801; 1:1000 for WB), anti-RPL26 antibody (17619-1-AP; RRID: AB_2878420; 1:3000 for WB), anti-UBA5 antibody (12093-1-AP; RRID: AB_2211743; 1:1000 for WB), anti-UFSP2 antibody (16999-1-AP; RRID; AB_2214070; 1:1000 for WB), and anti-Ki-67 antibody (27309-1-AP, RRID: AB_2756525; 1:6000 for IHC (immunohistochemistry); 1:500 for IF (immunofluorescence)) were obtained from Proteintech. Anti-PKC alpha antibody (R014277), anti-Phospho-PKC alpha (Thr638) antibody (R014974; 1:1000 for WB), anti-PLK1 antibody (R011618; 1:1000 for WB), anti-Phospho-PLK1 (Thr210) antibody (R015061; 1:1000 for WB), and anti-PDK1 antibody (R013172; 1:1000 for WB) were purchased from Epizyme. Anti-AKT1 antibody (sc-5298; RRID; AB_626658; 1:1000 for WB), anti-SREBP1 antibody (sc-17755; RRID: AB_628283; 1:1000 for WB), anti-PDI antibody (sc-376370; RRID: AB_10988269; 1:200 for WB), and normal mouse IgG (sc-2025; RRID: AB_737182) were obtained from Santa Cruz Biotechnology. Anti-AKT1 antibody (2938; RRID; AB_915788; 1:1000 for WB; 1:100 for IF), anti-Phospho-Akt (Ser473) (D9E) antibody (4060; RRID: AB_2315049; 1:1000 for WB; 1:200 for IHC), anti-Phospho-Akt (Thr308) (D25E6) antibody (13038; RRID: AB_2629447; 1:1000 for WB; 1:100 for IHC), anti-Phospho-ATP-Citrate Lyase (Ser455) antibody (4331; RRID: AB_2257987; 1:1000 for WB), anti-Phospho-(Ser/Thr) Akt Substrate antibody (9611; RRID: AB_330302; 1:800 for WB), normal rabbit IgG antibody (2729; RRID: AB_1031062), and anti-cleaved caspase 3 (Asp175) antibody (9661; RRID: AB_2341188; 1:100 for IF; 1:300 for IHC) were obtained from Cell Signaling Technology. HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit secondary antibody (AB0101; RRID: AB_2941855; 1:10000 for WB) and HRP-conjugated goat anti-mouse antibody (AB0102; RRID: AB_2904147; 1:10,000 for WB) were obtained from Abways. Anti-UFL1 antibody (HPA030559, RRID: AB_10600537; 1:1000 for WB; 1:100 for IHC; 1:150 for IF) and anti-Flag-M2 antibody (F1804; RRID: AB_262044; 1:5000 for WB) were obtained from Sigma-Aldrich. Anti-UFM1 antibody (ab109305; RRID: AB_10864675; 1:1000 for WB), anti-Calreticulin antibody (ab92516; RRID: AB_10562796; 1:300 for WB; 1:500 for IF) were obtained from Abcam. Alexa Fluor 488-conjugated donkey anti-rabbit secondary antibody (A21206; RRID: AB_2535792; 1:1000 for IF) and Alexa Fluor 594-conjugated donkey anti-mouse secondary antibody (A21203; RRID: AB_141633; 1:1000 for IF) were obtained from Thermo Fisher Scientific. For all immunoprecipitation (IP) assays, 1–4 μg primary antibody was incubated with 1–3 mg total protein.

Cell growth assays
Breast cancer cells (1 × 105) were suspended in medium supplemented with or without 20 μM oleic acid (OA) and seeded in 6-well plates (Jet Bio-Filtration, TCP011006). The cells at each time point were detached using 0.05% Trypsin-EDTA, resuspended in medium, stained with trypan blue, and counted using a TC20 automated cell counter (Bio-Rad).

Cell viability assays
Breast cancer cells (2 × 103) were seeded in 96-well plates (Jet Bio-Filtration, TCP011096). The next day, the cells were treated with 2 μM DMK 2-93 (MedChemExpress, HY-101836), 0.5 μM MK-2206 (MedChemExpress, HY-10358), 0.2 μM etoposide (Sigma, E1383), 2 μM or 1 μM cisplatin (Sigma, 232120), or a combination of these inhibitors for four days. Viable cells were measured using a Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8; MedChemExpress, HY-K0301) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Immunofluorescence staining
For antibody staining, breast cancer cells were washed twice with PBS and fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA, Sangon Biotech, E672002) at room temperature for 20 min. These cells were washed twice with PBS, permeabilized with 0.2% Triton X-100 solution for 20 min, and then blocked with 3% BSA at room temperature for 30 min. Subsequently, the cells were incubated overnight with primary antibodies at 4 °C. The next day, cells were washed with PBS and incubated with secondary antibodies for 1 hour at room temperature. To analyze protein colocalization, Pearson’s correlation coefficients (Rr) were calculated using the Fiji Colocalization Finder plugin in ImageJ software. The Rr values represent colocalization (0.5 < r < 1.0) or no colocalization (−1 < r < 0.5). Additionally, the intensities of green and red were plotted in a scatter plot to visualize fluorescence colocalization. Liner and diagonal distributions indicate good colocalization. For BODIPY staining, after treatment with 1 mM sodium citrate for 12 h in the absence or presence of 1 μM Fatostatin (MedChemExpress, HY-14452A), 45 μM C75 (MedChemExpress, HY-12364), 50 μM JR-AB2-011 (MedChemExpress, HY-14452A), 6 μM MK-2206 (MedChemExpress, HY-12464), or 20 μM DKM 2-93 (MedChemExpress, HY-122022), breast cancer cells were washed with PBS after fixation and stained with 0.25 μg/mL BODIPY 493/503 (Thermo Fisher, D3922) for 15 min. Finally, cells were stained with DAPI (Sigma-Aldrich, 10236276001). Immunofluorescence images were captured using a Leica TCS SPE confocal microscope (Leica). Quantification of BODIPY average intensity was performed using Image-Pro Plus (Media Cybermetics).

Oil Red O (ORO) staining
For cell ORO staining, after treatment with 1 mM sodium citrate for 12 h, breast cancer cells were wash by PBS and fixed with 4% PFA (Sangon Biotech, E672002). The cells were then stained with ORO staining solution (Sangon Biotech, E607319) according to the standard protocol. To quantify lipid accumulation, ORO was eluted with 100% isopropanol, and the optical densities of the eluates were measured with a spectrophotometer at a wavelength of 510 nm. To visualize lipid accumulation in breast tumors, tumor was fixed in 4% PFA (Sangon Biotech, E672002) overnight at 4 °C and then sequentially dehydrated with 15% and 30% sucrose at 4 °C. Tumor tissues were embedded in Tissue-Tek OCT compound and frozen in 2-methylbutane precooled with liquid nitrogen. Afterward, tissues were sectioned into 10 μm thick slides using a cryostat microtome. Tumor sections were placed on SuperFrost glass slides, air-dried, and soaked in 60% isopropanol for 5 min, followed by incubation in ORO solution (Sangon Biotech, E607319) according to the standard protocol. Sections were then decolorized in 60% isopropanol solution for 20 s, washed three times with ddH2O, and incubated in hematoxylin for 10 s. The slides were rinsed three times with ddH2O, air-dried, and sealed with glycerol-gelatin mounting solution. Images were captured using a Leica microscope. Quantification of ORO intensity in tumors was performed using Image-Pro Plus (Media Cybermetics).

Flow cytometry
The experimental procedure for detecting apoptosis was performed using an Annexin-V-YS Fluor 647/PI Apoptosis Detection Kit (YEASEN, 40304ES). Briefly, cells were harvested using trypsin (EDTA-free), washed twice with cold PBS, and resuspended at a density of 1 × 106 cells/mL in 100 μL 1X Annexin-V binding buffer. Subsequently, the cell suspension was incubated with 5 μL YS Fluor 647-conjugated Annexin-V and 10 μL propidium iodide (PI) for 15 min at room temperature in the dark. Following the incubation, 400 μL binding buffer was added to each sample. The stained cells were then immediately analyzed using a flow cytometer (BD Biosciences, LSR Fortessa), collecting a minimum of 10,000 events per sample. Median fluorescence intensity was used for statistical analyses to mitigate the influence of outliers and skewed distributions. The resulting data was interpreted using FlowJo software (BD Biosciences, version 11) to distinguish viable (Annexin-V⁻/PI⁻), early apoptotic (Annexin-V⁺/PI⁻), late apoptotic (Annexin-V⁺/PI⁺), and necrotic or damaged cells (Annexin-V⁻/PI⁺) based on their differential fluorescence signals in the FL1 and FL2 channels.

Immunoprecipitation and immunoblotting
Cells were resuspended in NETN lysis buffer (150 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 10 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0, 0.5% NP-40, protease inhibitors, and phosphatase inhibitors), followed by sonication and centrifugation at 12,000 g for 10 min. Whole-cell lysates were subjected to immunoblotting (IB) analysis. For immunoprecipitation assays, cell lysates were incubated with the indicated antibodies and protein A/G magnetic beads (Bio-Rad) or PIP3 coated magnetic beads (Echelon Biosciences, P-B345A) at 4 °C overnight. Subsequently, the beads were gently washed three times with NETN lysis buffer. The immunoprecipitates were boiled in 1 x Laemmli buffer and separated by SDS-PAGE. IB was subsequently performed using the indicated antibodies.

Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) assay
MDA-MB-231 cells stably expressing Flag-UFL1, treated with MG132 for 6 h before harvest, were lysed using NETN lysis buffer. The supernatant was collected and incubated with anti-Flag magnetic beads (BioLinkedIn, L1103) at 4 °C for 2 h. The putative UFL1-interacting proteins in the immunoprecipitates were fractionated by SDS-PAGE and subjected to LC-MS/MS analysis conducted by PTM Biolabs Inc. Briefly, the tryptic peptides were analyzed using an NSI source, followed by MS/MS in a Q ExactiveTM Plus (Thermo) system coupled online to the EASY-Nlc 1000 UPLC system. The resulting MS/MS data were processed using Proteome Discoverer 1.3. Tandem mass spectra were searched against Homo Sapiens database (SwissProt, 20395 sequences). Trypsin/P was specified as the cleavage enzyme, allowing up to 2 missing cleavages. Mass error tolerance was set to 10 ppm for precursor ions and 0.02 Da for fragment ions. Carbamidomethyation on cysteine residues was specified as a fixed modification, and oxidation on methionine residues was specified as variable modification. Peptide confidence was set to high, and the peptide ion score threshold was set to > 20.

Protein purification and pull-down assay
Full-length and truncated GST-AKT1 proteins were expressed in BL21 competent E. coli cells and purified with glutathione-Sepharose 4B (GE Healthcare, 17-0756-01) following standard protocols. Purified GST or GST-fusion proteins were incubated with immunoprecipitated UFL1 from breast cancer cells. Subsequently, the beads were washed extensively five times, boiled in 1 x Laemmli buffer, and analyzed by IB to assess the protein interaction.

In vivo UFMylation assay
In vivo UFMylation assays were performed as described previously41,63. Briefly, HEK293T or breast cancer cells were collected and resuspended in a buffer containing 150 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 5% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS), and 30% glycerol, followed by boiling for 10 min. Cell lysates were diluted with buffer A (50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% NP-40, 2 mM N-ethylmaleimide, and proteinase inhibitors) at a 1:20 ratio and incubated with the indicated antibodies and protein A/G magnetic beads (Bio-Rad) at 4 °C overnight. The immunoprecipitates were boiled in 1 x Laemmli buffer, separated by SDS-PAGE, and analyzed by IB.

In vitro UFMylation assay
In vitro UFMylation assays were performed according to the previous description41. Briefly, HEK293T cells were co-transfected with plasmids encoding HA-UBA5, HA-UFC1, HA-UFBP1, and HA-UFM1, and lysed with NETN lysis buffer for immunoprecipitation using anti-HA magnetic beads, followed by elution with HA peptide. Meanwhile, Flag-UFL1 expressed in HEK293T cells was immunoprecipitated with anti-Flag magnetic beads and subsequently eluted with Flag peptide. GST or GST-AKT1 bound to glutathione-Sepharose 4B (GE Healthcare, 17-0756-01) was incubated with immunoprecipitated HA-UBA5, HA-UFC1, HA-UFBP1, HA-UFM1, and Flag-UFL1 in a buffer containing 0.05% bovine serum albumin, 50 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 5 mM ATP, and 10 mM MgCl2 at 30 °C for 2 h. The immunoprecipitates were boiled in 1x Laemmli buffer, separated by SDS-PAGE, and analyzed by IB.

In vivo phosphorylation assay
Breast cancer cells were lysed with NETN buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors. For AKT1 and ACLY, cell lysates were subjected to SDS-PAGE, followed by IB analysis using anti-p-AKT1 (S473), anti-p-AKT1 (T308), or anti-p-ACLY (S455) antibodies. For UFL1, endogenous UFL1 or exogenous Flag-UFL1 was immunoprecipitated using anti-UFL1 or anti-Flag antibody, respectively. Immunoprecipitated UFL1 or Flag-UFL1 was subjected to SDS-PAGE, followed by IB analysis using anti-p-AKT-sub or anti-p-UFL1 (T426) antibodies.

In vitro phosphorylation assay
Immunoprecipitated UFL1 from breast cancer cells was mixed with purified GST or GST-AKT1 in 1x kinase buffer (25 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 5 mM beta-glycerophosphate, 2 mM dithiothreitol (DTT), 0.1 mM Na3VO4, 10 mM MgCl2, and 100 mM ATP), and incubated at 37 °C for 2 h. The mixture was separated by SDS-PAGE, followed by IB analysis using specific antibodies.

Reverse transcription (RT)-qPCR
Total RNA was isolated from cultured cells using Trizol reagent (Invitrogen, 15596018) and treated with DNase I (Ambion, AM2224). cDNA was synthesized using iScript Reverse Transcription Supermix (BioRad, 1708841). RT-qPCR assays were performed in triplicate using Hieff qPCR SYBR Green Master Mix (YEASEN, 11201ES08) according to the standard protocol. Primers for RT-qPCR were obtained from PrimerBank (https://pga.mgh.harvard.edu/primerbank/): ACLY (Fw: ATCGGTTCAAGTATGCTCGGG; Rv: GACCAAGTTTTCCACGACGTT), FASN (Fw: ACAGCGGGGAATGGGTACT; Rv: GACTGGTACAACGAGCGGAT), ACC1 (Fw: CATGCGGTCTATCCGTAGGTG; Rv: GTGTGACCATGACAACGAATCT), SCD1 (Fw: TCTAGCTCCTATACCACCACCA; Rv: TCGTCTCCAACTTATCTCCTCC), ACSS2 (Fw: CAAGTGTGTCAGTTCAGCAATG; Rv: CCACAAGCTCTGGGATCATAGG), CD36 (Fw: CCAAGCTCTGGGATCATAGG, Rv, GCATTTGCTGATGTCTAGCACA), FATP2 (Fw: TTTCCGCCATCTACACAGTCC; Rv: CGTAGGTGAGAGTCTCGTCG), FATP5 (Fw: CATGGCGTGACAGTGATCCT; Rv: CAGCCCGTAGTCCATTGCC), CPT1 (Fw: TCCAGTTGGCTTATCGTGGTG; Rv: TCCAGAGTCCGATTGATTTTTGC), CPT2 (Fw: CTGGAGCCAGAAGTGTTCCAC; Rv: AGGCACAAAGCGTATGAGTCT), ACOX1 (Fw: ACTCGCAGCCAGCGTTATG; Rv: AGGGTCAGCGATGCCAAAC), LDLR (Fw: ACGGCGTCTCTTCCTATGACA; Rv: CCCTTGGTATCCGCAACAGA), MTTP (Fw: ATTGTAAAGTGACCTACCAGGCT; Rv: ACCTCGCTATTTTGCATGAATCC), 18S (Fw: CGCGGTTCTATTTTGTTGGT; Rv: AGTCGGCATCGTTTATGGTC), RPL13A (Fw: GAGGTCGGGTGGAAGTACCA; Rv: TGCATCTTGGCCTTTTCCTT).

Cytosol and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) isolation
ER was isolated according to an optimized approach65. Briefly, breast cancer cells were washed with PBS, resuspended in ice-cold MIB-S buffer (0.25 M D-Sucrose, 25 mM KCl, 10 mM HEPES, 1 mM EGTA (pH 8.0)), centrifuged at 600 g for 5 min, and homogenized using a 15 cm3 homogenizer with a tight pestle for 20 strokes. Cell lysates were centrifuged at 600 g for 5 min, and supernatant I was collected. Supernatant I was centrifuged at 1200 g for 5 min, and supernatant II was retained. Supernatant II was centrifuged at 20,000 g for 35 min, and supernatant III was retained. Supernatant III was centrifuged at 100,000 g for 65 min, and supernatant IV (cytosol) and the ER pellet were kept for protein detection.

Quantification of free fatty acid (FFA) and total cholesterol
The content of FFA and total cholesterol were quantified using the FFA content assay kit (Solarbio, BC0595) and the total cholesterol content assay kit (Solarbio, BC1985), respectively. Briefly, breast cancer cells were resuspended in extraction solutions and sonicated, and the supernatant was collected. Absorbance of the supernatant was measured using a microplate reader at 545 nm for FFA and 500 nm for total cholesterol. All experiments were conducted in triplicate, and the data were normalized to cell numbers.

Animal studies
Animal studies were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at Shandong Normal University (SDNU). Female nonobese diabetic-severe combined immunodeficiency (NOD-SCID) mice (6–8 weeks old, Strain NO. T001492) were purchased from GemPharmatech and housed in a specific pathogen-free (SPF) facility, where they were maintained on a 12-h light/12-h dark cycle at a controlled ambient temperature of 20–24 °C and relative humidity of 40–60%. According to the policy of the IACUC at SDNU, the volume of xenograft tumors in mice should not exceed 2000 mm3. 2 × 106 MDA-MB-231 or MDA-MB-468 cells, resuspended in 50 μL PBS, were mixed with an equal volume of Matrigel (ABW Bio, 82704) and injected into the second left mammary fat pad of female NOD-SCID mice. To assess the effect of Fatostatin, DKM 2-93, and MK-2206, MDA-MB-231 tumor (approximately 100 mm3)-bearing mice were randomly assigned to four treatment groups (five mice per group) and received either a vehicle solution (2% DMSO, 40% PEG 400, 5% Tween-80, and 53% saline), Fatostatin (30 mg/kg, intraperitoneal, once every three days), MK-2206 (100 mg/kg, oral, once every three days), DKM 2-93 (40 mg/kg, intraperitoneal, once every three days), or a combination of MK-2206 and DKM 2-93. Tumor size was measured every three days with a caliper when tumor size reached approximately 100 mm3 and analyzed according to the formula: V=0.52 × L × H × W (V: volume, L: length, H: height, W: width). Mice were euthanized with carbon dioxide, and primary tumors were surgically removed, weighted, and photographed when their volume reached approximately 1500 mm3 in any cohort.

Immunohistochemistry (IHC)
IHC assays were performed as described previously66. Briefly, tumors were fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin, paraffin-embedded, and sectioned. Tissue ribbons were placed onto slides, which were then baked, deparaffinized using xylene, and hydrated in graded ethanol, followed by antigen retrieval in Citrate Antigen Retrieval solution. Endogenous peroxidase activity was blocked with 3% peroxide-methanol, and non-specific staining was blocked with 10% goat serum. The tissues were incubated with the indicated primary antibodies overnight at 4 °C and followed by HRP-conjugated secondary antibody for 1 h at room temperature. The following primary antibodies were used: anti-Ki-67 (1:5000), anti-cleaved caspase-3 (CC3, 1:500), anti-AKT1 (1:100), anti-p-AKT1 (S473) (1:100), anti-p-AKT1 (T308) (1:100), anti-UFL1 (1:150), and anti-p-UFL1 (T426) (1:150). The staining was visualized using the Pannoramic MiDi II slide scanner (3D Histech, Budapest, Hungary). The number of CC3-positive cells or Ki-67-positive cells per field was counted manually, and the average intensity (integrated intensity/area) of AKT1, p-AKT1 (S473), anti-p-AKT1 (T308), UFL1, and p-UFL1 (T624) in xenograft tumors was determined using Image-Pro Plus (Media Cybermetics). The human breast tumor tissue microarrays (TMAs) consisting of 120 human breast cancer tissues and 46 adjacent normal breast tissues were purchased from the Tissue Resource at The First Affiliated Hospital of Jinan University, which provided only the status of ER (estrogen receptor), HER2 (human epidermal growth factor receptor 2), and PR (progesterone receptor) of breast cancer tissues. Ethical approval (JNUKY-2023-0062, 2023/01/01-2026/12/31) and informed consent have been obtained regarding the use of patient tissues. The IHC staining of TMAs was quantitatively scored by Drs. Yan Chen and Junjie Liang on a four-grades scale (0–3) based on the percentage of positive cells and the overall staining intensity, as previously described67. The sections were assigned by the following proportion scores: 0 if 0% of the tumor cells displayed positive staining, 1 for 0–1%, 2 for 2–10%, 3 for 11–30%, 4 for 31–70%, 5 for 71–100%. Additionally, the intensity of staining was assigned a four-graded scale (0–3). Grades 0–3 represent: no expression (0), weak expression (1), moderate expression (2), and strong expression (3). A total score (range, 0–8) was obtained by combining the proportion and intensity scores. GraphPad Prism 8.0 was employed to perform the Pearson correlation analysis (two-tailed). Note that the scores for some samples overlap.

Statistical analysis
At least 3 samples prepared from independent experiments were used to ensure adequate power for all studies. Statistical analysis was carried out by one-way or two-way ANOVA with multiple testing correlation within multiple groups, two-tailed t-test within two groups, two-tailed Pearson correlation test, or log-rank test. Data were presented as mean ± SD. Significance was established at p < 0.05.
