Response to Editor and Reviewers
Editor and Reviewers’ comments are highlighted in blue, and the response is provided below the
referee comments.
Reviewer #1 (AKT activation and posttranslational modifications, Remarks to the Author):
Summary:
This manuscript from Fei Meng et al presents a mechanistic study uncovering a positive feedback loop
between UFL1 and AKT1 in triple-negative breast cancer. The authors show that UFL1 promotes AKT1
activation through UFMylation at lysines K189, K276, and K297, facilitating AKT1’s ER localization
and interaction with upstream kinases PDK1 and mTORC2. In turn, AKT1 phosphorylates UFL1 at
T426, enhancing UFL1 activity and thereby amplifying UFMylation. This regulatory axis is shown to
control lipid metabolism and tumor growth, and the study further demonstrates that pharmacological
inhibition of UFMylation sensitizes cells to AKT inhibition and chemotherapy. These mechanistic
findings came from a comprehensive and rigorous experimental design, in which the authors combined
in vitro biochemistry, genetic models and in vivo xenograft mouse model. Moreover, the identification
and functional dissection of UFMylation (3K/R) and phosphorylation (T426) sites are well executed
and supported by multiple lines of evidence. The use of AKT and UFMylation inhibitors, and the
demonstration of synergy, provide a translational angle that strengthens the manuscript. Finally, the
emphasis on AKT1-mediated lipid accumulation connects this signaling axis to a well-established
hallmark of cancer. However, several key points need to be addressed to fully support the proposed
model.
Major Points for Revision:
1. Biochemical Evidence for AKT1 UFMylation in AKT activation: A key mechanistic claim of the
manuscript is that UFMylation of AKT1 at K189, K276, and K297 is required for its phosphorylation
at T308 and S473. However, in standard cellular models (including our own lab’s experience and
1
widely published studies), insulin or IGF-1 stimulation induces robust AKT1 phosphorylation without
any observable upward shift in AKT1 molecular weight on Western blot with the phospho-AKT1
specific antibodies. This raises an important question: if UFMylation were required for AKT
activation, why is the fully activated AKT with both p-T308 and p-S473 readily observed in the
absence of a UFM1-dependent band shift in these common settings? Please clarify whether the
proposed UFL1-AKT1 UFMylation axis is prior to AKT activation and whether the de-UFMylation of
fully activated AKT1 happened.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these constructive suggestions.
(1). Based on our findings that UFL1 depletion, UBA5 ablation, and mutation of AKT’s UFMylation
sites (3K/R) all significantly decreased AKT phosphorylation (Fig. 4A, B; Supplementary Fig. 4A-C
in the revised manuscript), we concluded that AKT UFMylation occurs prior to AKT phosphorylation.
(2). We agree that insulin or IGF-1-activated AKT1 displays no changes to its molecular weight, which
seems to conflict with the fact that UFMylation is required for AKT activation and UFM1’s molecular
weight is approximately 9 kDa. We hypothesized that AKT phosphorylation promotes its
deUFMylation. To address this, we performed the following experiments, and these results support
our prediction from different angles.
(i). Similar to other post-translational modifications, UFMylation is dynamic and reversible, and this
feature ensures that UFMylated AKT1 accounts for a tiny portion of total AKT1. Therefore,
endogenous AKT1 and p-S473 were examined using an anti-AKT1 antibody or an anti-p-S473 antibody
in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells with or without UFL1 depletion. After a long exposure,
weak p-S473 and AKT1 bands, whose molecular weights were approximately 27 kDa greater than that
of their corresponding lower bands due to UFMylation at K189, K276, and K297, were observed in
shSC cells, and these upper bands nearly disappeared in UFL1 knockdown cells (Supplementary Fig.
4K in the revised manuscript). Hence, a tiny amount of AKT1 is maintained in a UFMylation state,
perhaps due to deUFMylation.
2
[FIGURE REDACTED]
(ii). Covalently bound UFM1 is primarily cleaved from substrates by the cysteine protease UFSP2
(Christopher P. Walczak et al., 2019 PNAS. PMID: 30626644; Jessie Kulsuptrakul et al., 2021 Cell
Rep. PMID: 33730579)(Fig. 1 in this letter). Thus, UFSP2 was depleted by shRNA in MDA-MB-231
and MDA-MB-468 cells to assess whether inhibited deUFMylation leads to an increase in AKT1
UFMylation and an upward shift of the p-S473 band. As expected, the intensity of the upper p-S473
band and the UFMylated AKT1 band was both significantly increased in UFSP2 knockdown cells (Fig.
4H in the revised manuscript). These findings indicate that AKT1 undergoes deUFMylation.
(iii). p-T308 and p-S473 result in full AKT1 activation. A plasmid encoding a mutant AKT1 (referred
to as AKT1-DM), which harbors T308A and S473A mutations, was generated. MDA-MB-231 cells
expressing comparable levels of wild-type (AKT1-WT) and AKT1-DM were established. Compared
with AKT1-WT, AKT1-DM possessed higher levels of UFMylation (Fig. 4I in the revised manuscript),
suggesting that AKT1 phosphorylation enhances its deUFMylation.
(iv). Breast cancer cells expressing AKT1-WT and AKT1-DM were treated with or without insulin and
subjected to co-immunoprecipitation (co-IP) assays. The interaction between UFSP2 and AKT1-WT
was stronger than the UFSP2-AKT1-DM association, and the former, but not the latter, interaction was
3
increased by insulin treatment (Fig. 4J in the revised manuscript). Hence, AKT1 phosphorylation
promotes the UFSP2-AKT1 interaction.
Collectively, these findings indicate that AKT1 UFMylation promotes AKT1 phosphorylation, which
in turn enhances the UFSP2-AKT1 interaction, thereby deUFMylating AKT1.
Notably, a similar phenomenon has been reported in AKT1 polyubiquitination (Wei-Lei Yang et al.,
C H Lin, S Y Liu, and E H Y Lee, 2016 Oncogene. PMID: 25867063), which significantly increase
AKT1’s molecular weight, while p-T308 and p-S473 bands with an upward shift are barely detectable.
Further investigations are needed to clarify whether ubiquitination, SUMOylation, and other post-
translational modifications of AKT1 are also removed by de-conjugation enzymes after AKT1 is
phosphorylated.
2. Breast cancer subtype specificity: While experiments include multiple breast cancer subtypes, the
core mechanistic and therapeutic data focus largely on TNBC cell lines. Some conclusions imply pan-
breast cancer relevance, but the experimental data supporting this are relatively limited. Please clarify
whether the UFL1-AKT1 feedback loop and its impact on lipid metabolism are broadly active across
subtypes, or primarily relevant in TNBC.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these valuable comments. The UFL1 mRNA and protein levels
are both increased in all breast cancer subtypes, including Luminal A, Luminal B, HER2+, and TNBC
(Supplementary Fig. 1A, D in the revised manuscript). UFL1 ablation suppressed the proliferation of
all breast cancer cell types (Fig. 1G, H; Supplementary Fig. 1E-G in the revised manuscript). All these
findings indicate that the UFL1-AKT1 feedback loop and its impact on lipid metabolism may be
broadly active across subtypes. To further test this hypothesis, we carried out the following
experiments:
(1). MCF-7 (Luminal A), BT474 (Luminal B), and SK-BR-3 (HER2+) cells were transfected with
vectors encoding AKT1-WT or AKT1-3K/R and subjected to UFMylation detection. Our results
4
indicated that AKT1-WT, but not AKT1-3K/R, was UFMylated in MCF-7, BT474, and SK-BR-3 cells
(Supplementary Fig. 3N-P in the revised manuscript), suggesting that K189, K276, and K297 are key
UFMylation sites in Luminal A, Luminal B, and HER2+ breast cancer cells. Additionally, we found
that AKT1-WT, but not AKT1-3K/R, enhanced lipid abundance in these breast cancer cells, as
evidenced by BODIPY staining assays (Supplementary Fig. 5H-M in the revised manuscript).
(2) MCF-7, BT474, and SK-BR-3 cells stably expressing UFL1-WT or UFL1-T426A were lysed for
UFL1 phosphorylation detection using an antibody that specifically recognizes phosphorylated UFL1
at T426 (referred to as p-UFL1 (T426) antibody). As expected, phosphorylation signals were only
observed in UFL1-WT, but not UFL1-T426A (Supplementary Fig. 6A in the revised manuscript). Thus,
p-UFL1 (T426) also occurs in Luminal A, Luminal B, and HER2+ breast cancer cells. Furthermore,
UFL1-WT increased lipid accumulation in MCF-7 and BT474 cells, whereas UFL1-T426A had no
impact on these cells (Supplementary Fig. 6G-J in the revised manuscript).
Taken together, these findings suggest that the UFL1-AKT1 feedback loop-mediated lipid metabolism
applies to all breast cancer subtypes. However, as we mentioned in the revised manuscript, TNBC is
more aggressive and lacks effective therapeutic targets; therefore, we mainly focused on TNBC in this
study.
3. Clinical relevance and correlation analysis: The manuscript refers to a positive correlation between
pUFL1 and pAKT1 in breast tumor tissues. However, the correlation coefficient (r) and significance
(p-value) are not clearly presented in the main text or figure legends. Please include the quantitative
data (r, p-value) and consider moving the correlation plot to a main figure to better support the clinical
relevance of the proposed axis.
Response: We thank the reviewer for these constructive suggestions. We quantitatively rescored the
specimens according to the percentage of immunopositive cells and the staining intensity, as
previously described (Ke Wu et al., 2023 Nat Cell Biol, PMID: 37156912). The sections were assigned
the following proportion scores: 0 if 0% of the tumor cells displayed positive staining, 1 for 0-1%, 2
5
for 2-10%, 3 for 11-30%, 4 for 31-70%, 5 for 71-100%. Additionally, the intensity of staining was
assigned a four-grade scale (0-3). Grades 0-3 represent: no expression (0), weak expression (1),
moderate expression (2), and strong expression (3). A total score (range, 0-8) was obtained by
combining the proportion and intensity scores. GraphPad Prism 8.0 was employed to perform the
Pearson correlation analysis (two-tailed). We have included these informations in the “Materials and
Methods” section of the revised manuscript. Additionally, as suggested, we have moved the correlation
plot from Supplementary Fig. 6 to Fig. 6T to better support the clinical relevance of the proposed axis,
and the correlation coefficient (r) and significance (p-value) have been presented in the Fig. 6T in the
revised manuscript.
4.Functional role of UFMylation beyond AKT1: The focus is tightly centered on AKT1, but the authors
note that other components of the lipid metabolism and PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathway may interact with
UFL1. Please comment more fully on whether UFMylation of othercomponents (e.g., ACLY, SREBP1
regulators) may contribute to the lipid phenotype, or whether this is uniquely AKT1-driven.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this recommendation. Rictor is a critical component of the
mTORC2 complex, and FASN catalyzes the conversion of Acetyl-CoA and Malonyl-CoA into long-
chain saturated fatty acids. Thus, they are essential for lipid synthesis. Our LC-MS/MS analysis
showed that Rictor and FASN are potential UFL1-interacting proteins (Supplementary Fig. 3A in the
revised manuscript). Co-IP and western blotting assays showed that UFL1 associates with and
UFMylates FASN and Rictor (Supplementary Fig. 3R-W in the revised manuscript). Moreover, UFL1
overexpression elevated lipid abundance, and this elevation was reversed by the FASN inhibitor C75
and Rictor inhibitor JR-AB2-011 (Supplementary Fig. 5O-T in the revised manuscript), suggesting that
UFL1 modulates lipid metabolism through multiple layers of mechanisms. Further investigations

The manuscript by Meng et al reported the critical role of the UFL1-AKT axis in breast cancer
progression and drug resistance. Specifically, the authors found that AKT1 was UFMylated by UFL1,
an UFMylation-specific E3 ligase, in breast cancer cells. AKT1 UFMylation promoted its ER
recruitment and activation by both PDK1 and mTORC2, which in turn enhanced lipid biogenesis and
cancer progression. Moreover, the authors showed that AKT1 phosphorylated UFL1 and boosted
UFL1’s activity. Finally, UFL1 expression was elevated in breast cancer samples and associated with
poor prognosis in human patients. Targeting both UFMylation and AKT1 had a synergetic effect on
TNBC in xenograft models.

and may represent a potential target for cancer therapy. However, there are some significant flaws in
data analysis and interpretation that should be addressed. As described below, this reviewer failed to
duplicate some of the results as claimed by the authors regarding the association between UFL1 mRNA
level and overall survival of human BC patients. In addition, a few pieces of experimental data
appeared to conflict to each other, and some results were difficult to explain. Finally, the evidence to
support the role of lipid metabolism in tumor progression is relatively insufficient.

17407381; Véronique Calleja, Michel Laguerre, and Banafshé Larijani, 2009 J Chem Biol. PMID:
19568789; R Meier et al., 1997 J Biol Chem. PMID: 9374542). From this perspective, all inactive AKT1
and most active AKT1 exist in the cytosol, and the influence of UFL1 depletion on the AKT1 levels in
the cytoplasmic fraction is negligible. In contrast, UFL1 depletion dramatically affected p-T308 and p-
S473 levels in both the cytosol and ER membrane.

6B in the revised manuscript) were both comparable in MDA-MB-231 and MDA-MB-468 cells
expressing UFL1-WT and UFL1-T426A, suggesting that p-UFL1 (T426) may specifically modulate
the AKT signaling pathway. Notably, AMPK phosphorylates UFL1 at T536, disrupting the UFL1-PD1

Response: Thank you for your constructive questions.
(1). Similar to your question #7, overall UFMylation was not affected by UBA5 and AKT inhibitors,
which may be due to two reasons: the specific lysis buffer for UFMylation detection was not fresh
enough, and too much protein was loaded for UFM1 detection. To avoid these problems, we repeated
all these assays using the following fresh lysis buffer: HEK293T or breast cancer cells were collected
and resuspended in a buffer containing 150 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 5% sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS),
and 30% glycerol, followed by boiling for 10 minutes.Cell lysates were diluted with buffer A (50 mM
Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 150 mM NaCl, 0.5% NP-40, 2 mM N-ethylmaleimide, and protease inhibitors) at a
1:20 ratio and incubated with the indicated antibodies and protein A/G magnetic beads (Bio-Rad) at
4 °C overnight. The immunoprecipitates were boiled in 1 x Laemmli buffer, separated by SDS-PAGE,
and analyzed by WB. For overall UFMylation (UFM1) detection, 5-10 μg of whole cell lysates were
loaded. In this case, a reduction in overall UFMylation was observed upon UFMylation inhibitor
treatment (Fig. 7A, B in the revised manuscript). Notably, UFL1 overexpression only had a minimal
impact on overall UFMylation (Supplementary Fig. 3I, J in the revised manuscript) probably due to
25
high levels and activity of endogenous UFL1 in breast cancer cells (Fig. 1C, D, Supplementary Fig. 1D;
Fig. 6T, Supplementary Fig. 6M in the revised manuscript).
(2). Synergistic combinations of two or more agents can overcome toxicity and other side effects
associated with high doses of single drugs by countering biological compensation, allowing reduced
dosage of each compound or accessing context-specific multitarget mechanisms (Joseph Lehár et al.,
Rev Cancer. PMID: 38627557). Multiple promising combinatorial strategies have been developed to
achieve synergistic effects, such as vertical inhibition, disruption of positive feedback loops, blocking
parallel signaling pathways, and preventing compensatory bypass signaling. ① Vertical inhibition
consists of inhibiting the main oncogenic driver, which is genetically altered, often mutated or
amplified, together with an upstream or downstream component of the same oncogenic pathway, to
achieve a deeper suppression of the pathway (Naiara Perurena, Lisa Situ, and Karen Cichowski, 2024
Nat Rev Cancer. PMID: 38627557; David Shahbazian, Joshua Sznol, and Harriet M Kluger, 2012 Adv
Pharmacol. PMID: 22959021). From this perspective, AKT1 is the main oncogenic driver, UFL1 (or
other components of the UFMylation system) is an upstream component of the AKT1 pathway; the
combination of an AKT1 inhibitor and a UBA5 inhibitor achieved a deeper suppression of the AKT1
pathway (Fig. 7 in the revised manuscript). Thus, the combination of an AKT1 inhibitor and a UBA5
inhibitor constitutes a vertical inhibition. Similarly, PDK1 phosphorylates AKT1 at T308, and a PDK1
inhibitor (GSK2334470) and an AKT1 inhibitor (Ipatasertib and MK-2206) achieve a synergistic effect
(Emily K Slotkin et al., 2019 Cancer Discov. PMID: 30877085; Kristyna Kupcova et al., 2024 Exp
Hematol Oncol. PMID: 39487517). PRMT5 methylates and subsequently activates AKT1, and a
PRMT5 inhibitor (GSK3326595) and an AKT inhibitor (MK-2206) display a synergistic effect on
promoting cell death (Shasha Yin et al., 2021 Nat Commun. PMID: 34103528). ② When Protein A
and Protein B directly or indirectly activate each other (forming a positive feedback loop), their
inhibitors frequently exhibit strong synergistic effects. This occurs because blocking either protein
26
alone leaves the other free to reactivate its partner, while dual inhibition almost collapses the entire
signaling circuit (Joseph Lehár et al., 2009 Nat Biotechnol. PMID: 19581876;Deborah Plana, Adam C
Palmer, and Peter K Sorger, 2022 Cancer Discov. PMID: 34983746). In this regard, AKT1 and UFL1
reciprocally activate each other to form a positive feedback loop; therefore, their inhibitors exert a
synergistic anti-cancer effect. In the same manner, an AKT inhibitor (MK-2206) and an mTOR
inhibitor (Everolimus) (Yvonne Yeung et al., 2017 Mol Oncol. PMID: 28544747), an EGFR inhibitor
(Gefitinib) and a MEK inhibitor (Trametinib) (João M Fernandes Neto et al., 2020 Nat Commun.
PMID: 32572029), and a STAT3 inhibitor (Napabucasin) and an IL-6 inhibitor (Tocilizumab) (Anibal
Méndez-Clemente et al., 2022 Oncol Rep. PMID: 35703345) exhibit synergistic anti-cancer effects. In
summary, the UBA5 inhibitor sensitizes breast cancer cells to the AKT1 inhibitor, and their
combination achieves a deeper suppression of AKT1 signaling and breast tumor growth, thereby
exhibiting a synergistic effect.
